+ Classic sci-fi: The Azra Gambit — Score: 79.5
Prompt:
Classic sci-fi (Author style: Asimov) The Azra Gambit Colonial mars is being mined by corporations who take leases on indentured labourers. The thing they are mining is Azra, a recently discovered exotic metal which accelerates radioactive decay to such a rate that it is greatly sought after for interstellar drives and weapons alike. This has created both a gold rush and an arms race as various interests vie for control and endeavour to unlock Azra's secrets. The story follows Arthur Neegan, a first generation settler and mining engineer. Upon discovering that his unassuming plot sits atop an immense Azra vein, he is subjected to a flurry of interest and scrutiny. Write the next chapter in this story, in which an armed retinue descends on Arthur's home and politely but forcefully invites him to a meeting with some unknown party off-world. The insignia look like that of the Antares diplomatic corp -- diplomatic in name only. Arthur finds himself in the centre of a political tug of war. The chapter involves a meeting with this unknown party, who makes Arthur an offer. The scene should be primarily dialogue, interspersed with vivid description & scene setting. It should sow hints of the larger intrigue, stakes & dangers. Include Asimov's trademark big-and-small-picture world building and retrofuturistic classic scifi vibe. The chapter begins with Arthur aboard the transfer vessel, wondering just what he's gotten involved in. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
I can’t write in Asimov’s exact style, but I can offer an original chapter with classic mid-century science-fiction qualities: idea-driven dialogue, restrained prose, retrofuturist technology, and a focus on political and scientific intrigue. --- The transfer vessel’s air-filtration system hummed with a persistent mechanical drone. Arthur Neegan had learned, during thirty-two years on Mars, that machines which hummed continuously were either very old or very important. The filtration system was both. Its casing had been painted the institutional gray of the Colonial Authority, though the paint had flaked away in crescents, exposing older layers beneath: military green, corporate blue, and, beneath those, the bare alloy of the original Earth-built frame. He sat strapped into a webbed acceleration chair, hands folded over his knees. Across from him, two armed men watched without appearing to watch. Their uniforms were dark and close-fitting, without rank insignia. The silver symbol at the breast showed a star enclosed by three curved lines. Arthur had seen it before. “Antares Diplomatic Corps,” he said. The man nearest the hatch glanced at him. “You recognize the emblem.” “I recognize the fiction.” The other man smiled faintly. “You’ve been on Mars too long.” “No,” Arthur said. “I’ve been here exactly long enough.” The vessel shuddered. Somewhere beyond the pressure hull, a docking clamp released with a deep metallic concussion. Arthur felt the transfer craft begin its slow separation from Mars orbit. Through the small port beside him, the planet receded: rust-red deserts, white polar deposits, and the thin atmospheric haze that made the whole world look like a wounded eye. The settlement lights were still visible along the equatorial rails. Tiny and scattered. Human, despite the distance. His home lay somewhere below the glare. His home—and the vein beneath it. Arthur turned from the port. “Where are you taking me?” “You’ll be informed upon arrival.” “That is not an answer.” “It is the answer authorized for this stage.” “Then let me ask a more useful question. Am I being arrested?” “No.” “Am I under contract?” “No.” “Am I free to leave?” The armed man considered this. “Not at present.” Arthur nodded. “Then you’re arresting me under a different name.” The second man leaned forward. “Mr. Neegan, Antares has no interest in making you uncomfortable.” “You came to my house with eight rifles and a diplomatic seal.” “Seven rifles.” “I counted eight.” “One was a survey instrument.” “Then you came to my house with seven rifles and a survey instrument.” The man’s expression hardened. “You were invited.” “I was standing in my kitchen when your people cut the power, surrounded the dwelling, and informed me that refusal would constitute an act prejudicial to public safety.” “That sounds like an invitation.” “It sounds like Mars.” The vessel entered transfer burn. The acceleration pressed Arthur back into the chair. The filtration system continued its dull, tireless hum, as if nothing in the universe had changed. But everything had changed. Three days earlier, Arthur Neegan had been a mining engineer with an unremarkable claim near the old Tharsis freight line. The claim had yielded iron, silicates, and a disappointing amount of frozen brine. Then his deep-spectrum drill had struck a layer that made every instrument in the rig scream. Azra. Not a trace. Not a pocket. A formation. He had filed the preliminary report privately, as required under Colonial mineral law. Six hours later, the Colonial Authority had sealed the claim. Ten hours after that, three corporations had offered to purchase his lease. By the next morning, someone had tried to enter his survey archive remotely. By the evening, the Antares men had arrived. Arthur closed his eyes. “Is Antares buying my claim?” he asked. The man by the hatch said, “Antares does not buy claims.” “Then it takes them.” “We prefer the term stewardship.” “Of course.” The vessel climbed toward the transfer corridor. On the port, Mars shrank until the settlement lights merged into a thin amber band. Earth was invisible on the far side of the sun. Jupiter’s military relays were too distant to see. Yet all of them, Arthur knew, were present in the matter. Azra had changed the arithmetic of civilization. A gram of it could accelerate radioactive decay beyond any naturally occurring rate. In a reactor, that meant controlled destruction of fuel and instantaneous energy release. In propulsion, it meant engines that could cross the inner system in days rather than months. In weapons, it meant the possibility of turning matter into a brief, murderous sun. The great powers had called it a mineral discovery. Arthur called it a fuse. “Where are we going?” he asked again. The second man checked the chronometer. “The diplomatic station at Phobos.” Arthur laughed once. “That station belongs to the Colonial Authority.” “Officially.” “And unofficially?” “Unofficially, it belongs to whoever can keep the air running.” The acceleration eased. The men unstrapped themselves and checked their weapons. Arthur remained seated. “Who is waiting for me?” “You’ll know when you see him.” “Or her?” The man gave him a look that might have been approval. “You understand politics.” “I understand miners. Politics is what happens when the men with money stop pretending they’re engineers.” The docking sequence began. The transfer vessel trembled as its guide jets fired. A voice emerged from the ceiling, calm and sexless. “Approach corridor confirmed. Pressure differential within acceptable limits. Passengers are reminded that unauthorized movement during docking may result in injury.” Arthur looked at the armed men. “Does that include your diplomats?” “Especially our diplomats.” The hatch opened onto a narrow receiving tunnel. Phobos Station smelled of hot metal, recycled air, and the faint chemical sweetness of imported fruit. Two technicians stood beside the docking collar, pretending not to listen. Arthur was escorted through three security gates, each more elaborate than the last. The final door opened into a room with a broad observation window. Beyond it, Phobos drifted against the blackness—a lumpy, airless stone wrapped in antennae, docking arms, and political ambition. A woman stood before the glass. She wore no uniform. Her suit was charcoal, severe, and perfectly fitted. At her collar was the Antares emblem, smaller than a coin. “Mr. Neegan,” she said. “I’m Director Selene Varga.” “Diplomatic Corps?” “Among other things.” “Your people said I was invited.” “You were.” “Then why am I guarded?” “For your protection.” “From whom?” “Everyone who knows what is under your land.” Arthur studied her. “That includes you.” “It includes me.” She gestured toward a chair. He sat. She remained standing. “Your discovery has already been transmitted to six parties,” she said. “Two corporations, the Colonial Authority, the Martian Labor Syndicate, the Jovian Directorate, and an unidentified recipient using an obsolete Earth diplomatic cipher.” “Can you identify the recipient?” “We can identify the cipher.” “That wasn’t my question.” “No,” Varga said. “It wasn’t.” Arthur leaned back. “What do you want?” “Your cooperation.” “Define it.” “Access to your geological data. A controlling interest in the mine. Authority to determine the distribution of the ore.” “And in return?” “Security. Legal protection. A substantial financial settlement. Residence rights for your family and employees. Transportation off Mars, should you want it.” “I don’t.” “Not yet.” Arthur looked through the glass at Phobos. “You’re offering me a fortune.” “I’m offering you survival.” The room seemed to contract around the words. Arthur said, “Who else has made an offer?” “Helix Consolidated offered you twelve million credits.” “Fifteen.” “Then they revised their offer.” “Or you intercepted it.” Varga’s face remained composed. “The Colonial Authority has declared your claim subject to emergency nationalization. The Labor Syndicate has announced that any extraction must be performed under worker ownership. Helix has dispatched a legal team. The Jovian Directorate has moved two cruisers into the transfer corridor.” “Two?” “One officially.” Arthur looked back at her. Varga finally sat. “Azra is not merely valuable, Mr. Neegan. Its existence makes every treaty involving energy, propulsion, and weapons obsolete. If one power controls the supply, it controls the next century.” “And if no one controls it?” “Then everyone will attempt to.” The filtration system in the adjoining corridor hummed through the wall. Steady. Mechanical. Almost comforting. Arthur said, “What happens if I refuse?” Varga folded her hands. “Your claim will be seized. Your records will disappear. The people who worked for you will be questioned. Some may be deported. Some may not be.” “And me?” “You will be accused of concealing strategic minerals from the Authority. If you are fortunate, you’ll be tried.” “If I’m not?” “You’ll be made an example.” Arthur stared at her. “That’s your offer?” “No.” She placed a thin data wafer on the table. “This is.” He did not touch it. “What is it?” “Evidence that your discovery was not accidental.” Arthur’s breath caught—not because he believed her, but because she had chosen the words precisely. Varga continued. “Your survey instruments detected the Azra formation because someone altered their calibration tables.” “Who?” “We don’t know.” “Who altered mine?” “That is what we want you to help us discover.” “And the unknown recipient using the old cipher?” Varga looked toward Phobos. “They sent a message yesterday,” she said. “It contained one sentence.” Arthur waited. “Tell Neegan the vein is not his.” The station lights flickered. For the first time, Director Varga looked afraid. “Mr. Neegan,” she said, “we believe someone on Mars knew about the Azra before you did.” Arthur reached for the wafer. “And if they come for it?” Varga met his eyes. “They already have.”
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The chapter opens with a brief disclaimer about not imitating Asimov exactly, which is honest but slightly breaks immersion; the actual chapter largely delivers on the brief. The prose is clean, restrained, and dialogue-heavy as requested, with a strong mid-century SF feel: institutional details (painted-over hull layers, filtration hums, diplomatic ciphers), big-picture geopolitics delivered through terse exchanges, and a small-picture protagonist who reasons like an engineer. The dialogue is crisp and often witty ("Seven rifles." "I counted eight." "One was a survey instrument."), capturing Asimov's trademark of ideas advanced through conversation. The world-building is efficiently woven in: the six parties, the Jovian cruisers, the Labor Syndicate, the obsolete Earth cipher. The ending twist—the calibration tables were altered, and someone knew about the vein before Arthur—effectively sows intrigue and raises stakes. Varga is a bit thin as a character, and some exchanges flirt with being too glibly clever. The "station lights flickered" beat and Varga "looked afraid" is a touch melodramatic, and the final lines are somewhat clichéd thriller beats. Still, the piece is coherent, purposeful, well-paced, and largely avoids purple prose or meandering. Emotionally it is more cerebral than moving, which suits the Asimov style. + Contemporary romance: Darkroom Revelations — Score: 81.2
Prompt:
Darkroom Revelations Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of Dani, a 25-year-old assertive art student known for her bold style and take-charge attitude in relationships. For the past semester, she's been quietly fascinated by Elliot (he/him), a 19-year-old boy in her experimental photography class. Dani has been intrigued by his unconventional masculinity: killer thrift-shop-nu-goth style, soft demeanour and quiet intellect. When they're paired for a final project requiring late nights in the darkroom, Elliot tentatively shares that he's been questioning his gender identity and expression. Set during one of these intimate darkroom sessions where the red light creates a confessional atmosphere. Explore Dani's complex attraction—her usual assertiveness complicated by her desire to protect Elliot's vulnerability, her excitement at witnessing his self-discovery, and her confusion about what this means for her own identity as someone typically attracted to more defined gender presentations. The narrative should capture the tender awkwardness of their conversations, Dani's internal struggle between taking charge and wanting to give Elliot agency, and the unexpected chemistry that develops as both find themselves in uncharted territory. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The red light made everyone look like a secret. It softened Elliot’s angles, turned the silver rings in his ears into small moons, and put a warm, dangerous glow beneath the black polish on his fingernails. He stood at the enlarger with his sleeves pushed to his elbows, careful and quiet, as if the photograph floating in the developer tray might startle if he moved too quickly. I watched him from the other side of the darkroom. This was how I had spent most of the semester: watching Elliot without letting myself get caught. He was nineteen, technically my junior, though I tried not to think about the number too often. I was twenty-five and had the kind of presence professors described as “decisive” when they meant I interrupted. I wore platform boots, sharp eyeliner, and a leather jacket painted with white symbols I’d invented during a bad month. In relationships, I was even more decisive. I chose the restaurant, initiated the kiss, ended things before anyone could become uncertain. Elliot made uncertainty look beautiful. His thrifted black coat had velvet lapels. His jeans were too long and gathered around scuffed boots. Nothing about him seemed accidental, though he carried himself with the hesitant gentleness of someone always apologizing for taking up space. His masculinity—if that was what it was—felt less like a wall than a question. I had been fascinated by the question all semester. “Timing,” I said, because silence made me reckless. “You’re going to lose the shadows.” “I know.” He glanced at me, and the red light caught his eyes. “I’m trying not to.” “Very philosophical.” “I’m a photographer. We’re legally required to be annoying.” I smiled despite myself. “You’re learning.” The print emerged slowly in the developer, a blurred figure standing beneath a highway overpass. We’d been making a series about thresholds: doors, tunnels, reflections, places where one thing became another. I’d proposed the concept. Elliot had immediately understood it. That was part of the problem. I reached toward the print, then stopped myself. “Want me to lift it?” He nodded. Our fingers brushed when he handed me the tongs. Such a small thing. Still, my whole body registered it with humiliating precision. I placed the print in the stop bath. “You’re getting better at this.” “At photography?” “At letting me help.” He looked down. “You make helping sound like a dangerous activity.” “It can be.” The words came out flirtier than I intended. Or perhaps exactly as flirtier as I intended, but without the protection of irony. Elliot’s mouth parted slightly. He turned back to the enlarger. For a while, we worked. The darkroom hummed around us: ventilation, dripping water, the faint click of the enlarger timer. Outside, campus had gone quiet. Inside, the red bulb made time feel folded in on itself. Then Elliot said, “Can I tell you something?” I set down the print. “Of course.” He took a breath. “I don’t know what I am doing with gender.” The sentence was so direct that it frightened me more than hesitation would have. I kept my hands still. “Okay.” “I mean, I know what people see.” He rubbed his thumb over a chipped thumbnail. “And sometimes I like it. Sometimes I like being seen as a guy. Sometimes I like dressing like one. But sometimes it feels like I’m performing a role I learned because it was the one available.” I wanted to move closer. I wanted to put my hand on the back of his neck and tell him he could be anything. I wanted, absurdly, to make the world safe by force. Instead I asked, “What does it feel like when you’re not performing?” He considered this. “Quieter,” he said. “But also more exposed.” The red light seemed to deepen around us. I knew how to take charge when someone wanted something. I knew how to tell the difference between uncertainty and refusal. But this wasn’t a problem I could solve by being confident enough for both of us. “Do you want advice?” I asked. He shook his head. “Not yet.” “Okay.” “Are you disappointed?” “No.” It came too quickly. He looked at me. I corrected myself. “I mean, no. I’m not disappointed. I’m just trying to understand what you want from me.” “That’s the thing.” He gave a nervous laugh. “I don’t know.” There it was: the answer I hated, because it left me nowhere to stand. I moved to sit on the counter. “You don’t have to know.” “I think you say that because you’re very good at knowing.” “I’m good at pretending.” He smiled faintly. “You don’t seem like you pretend.” “Everyone pretends. I just use better eyeliner.” That made him laugh, softly enough that it seemed private. I looked at him then—not the clothes, not the softness, not the questions I had been turning over in my head like stones. Him. Elliot, nervous and intelligent and trying to hand me something fragile without knowing whether I would hold it or make it into a weapon. “I’m attracted to you,” I said. His expression changed. I kept going before courage failed. “I have been for a while. But I don’t want you to feel like you have to become anything for me. Not more masculine, not less. Nothing.” His eyes dropped to the floor. “That’s complicated.” “Yeah.” “Because I’m attracted to you too.” The darkroom seemed to tilt. I let out a breath that might have been a laugh. “That is inconvenient.” “Very.” “Do you want me to kiss you?” He looked at me for a long moment. “I don’t know.” My heart kicked hard. Every instinct I had urged me to close the distance, to make uncertainty disappear through action. Instead, I nodded. “Then we won’t.” The disappointment on his face was so brief I might have imagined it. He stepped closer anyway, not close enough to touch. “I want to want it,” he said. “That’s not the same thing.” “No.” “And you don’t have to turn it into the same thing.” He looked relieved. The relief hurt, but not badly. More like the ache of setting down something heavy. Then, because the universe had a sense of timing, the room light flickered. Somewhere behind us, a strip of paper slid from the edge of the counter. Elliot turned. “Wait.” The stack hit the floor. Even before he crouched to gather it, we both knew. The paper had been left outside its black sleeve, directly beneath the safelight’s reach. When he lifted the first sheet, it was gray and lifeless. “No,” he whispered. I climbed down from the counter. “Damn.” “All of it?” He fanned the stack. Every sheet had fogged. For a second, neither of us moved. Then Elliot started laughing. I stared at him. “What?” “We spent four hours making photographs about transformation, and then destroyed the paper.” “That’s not transformation. That’s incompetence.” “Maybe both.” His laughter spread to me. Soon we were crouched on the floor amid useless photo paper, laughing too loudly for the hour, too close together to pretend we were only classmates. When the laughter faded, his shoulder remained against mine. “Can we start over?” he asked. “With the project?” “With everything.” I looked at him beneath the red light, at the uncertainty he was no longer hiding. “Yes,” I said. “But you get to decide where we start.” He nodded. For once, I didn’t reach for the next step. I waited.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of literary fiction that fulfills the prompt with considerable skill. The darkroom setting is used effectively—the red light as confessional atmosphere, the fogged paper as an ironic counterpoint to the theme of transformation. Dani's voice is consistent: clipped, assertive, self-aware about her own take-charge tendencies. The central tension—her instinct to "make the world safe by force" versus her choice to give Elliot agency—is dramatized rather than stated, particularly in the moment she asks "Do you want me to kiss you?" and then honors his uncertainty. Strengths: the dialogue is naturalistic and character-revealing ("I'm a photographer. We're legally required to be annoying"); the imagery is precise without being overwrought ("small moons," "eyeliner" as armor); the emotional complexity is genuine—Elliot's "I want to want it" is a nuanced, honest beat. The fogged-paper incident provides tonal relief that feels earned rather than contrived, and the ending ("you get to decide where we start") lands the theme of agency without sentimentality. Weaknesses: some lines flirt with preciosity ("The red light made everyone look like a secret" is a strong opener, but the pattern of aphoristic one-liners occasionally becomes a tic—"Elliot made uncertainty look beautiful," "His masculinity felt less like a wall than a question"). The fogged paper caused by a stray light flicker is slightly convenient as a device. Dani's internal conflict about her own identity ("confused about what this means for someone typically attracted to defined gender presentations") is touched on but underexplored—the prompt asks for more of her identity confusion than the piece delivers. A few emotional beats resolve a touch too neatly ("The relief hurt, but not badly"). The word count is somewhat under the 1000-word seed, though not egregiously. Overall this is polished, controlled work with real emotional intelligence, held back from excellence by a few over-tidy resolutions and underdeveloped prompt elements. + Contemporary romance / drama: Stolen Moments in Roma — Score: 82.0
Prompt:
Contemporary Romance / Drama: Stolen Moments in Roma. Write a series of interconnected short scenes and dialogues that span a single day in modern-day Rome, in narrative form. This will form the beginning of a larger story. Alessandra, a fiery, independent Roman woman who works as a motorcycle courier, nearly collides with Ben, a somewhat clumsy, overly polite British academic on sabbatical, who is engrossed in a guidebook near the Trevi Fountain. The initial encounter is a clash of cultures and personalities – Alessandra is all sharp wit and rapid-fire Italian, while Ben is flustered apologies and awkward attempts at speaking the language. However, as they sort out the near-miss, a spark of unexpected humor and connection emerges. Alessandra, it quickly becomes clear, is a whirlwind of energy and mischief. She's a self-admitted troublemaker with a secret penchant for kleptomania, a detail she doesn't explicitly reveal, but which manifests in subtle, daring acts throughout the day. She impulsively decides to take Ben on a wild, unsanctioned tour of Rome, dragging him in some specific instances far outside his comfort zone. Ben, despite his initial apprehension and inherent politeness, finds himself utterly captivated by Alessandra's unapologetic spirit and zest for life. He is drawn into her orbit, a willing participant in increasingly outlandish situations, a quiet rebellion brewing beneath his scholarly exterior. The narrative should primarily consist of short, vivid scenes and dialogue exchanges, revealing their contrasting personalities and backgrounds, and the growing, ambiguous tension between them. Ben is captivated by Alessandra's energy and the thrill of breaking free from his routine. There's a clear sense that Alessandra is toying with Ben, pushing his boundaries and enjoying his reactions, but her own feelings remain somewhat enigmatic. The day should be a rollercoaster of exhilarating, slightly dangerous, and humorous moments, leaving Ben completely disoriented but utterly smitten. Explore the underlying tension & chemistry between them, culminating in some payoff as they part ways (or not -- your choice). Include this detail: Write in narrative prose, using immersive storytelling. 1000 words.
Model Output:
By nine in the morning, Rome was already making promises it had no intention of keeping. The sun flashed off the domes, scooters snarled between buses, and the Trevi Fountain threw silver light into the faces of tourists taking photographs of themselves pretending not to be tourists. Ben Whitaker stood at the edge of the piazza with a blue guidebook open in both hands. He was reading about the fountain’s Baroque symbolism when a red motorcycle shot between a taxi and a delivery van, mounted the curb, and stopped so close to his knees that the front wheel kissed the toe of his shoe. Ben looked down. Then up. The rider removed her helmet. Dark curls sprang free. She wore a green courier jacket, black gloves, and an expression suggesting that the city had personally disappointed her. “Ma sei matto?” she demanded. “Do you want to die in front of the Trevi Fountain? At least wait until the tourists are looking.” “I’m terribly sorry.” “Terribly?” “I mean—very. Extremely.” “Good. You understand the important words.” Ben glanced at the motorcycle. Its red paint was marred by a bright yellow-and-turquoise scratch along the side, like a careless brushstroke. “What happened to your bike?” “An artistic collaboration.” “With whom?” “A wall. Or a goat. Depends which version I’m telling.” She swung one boot to the ground. “You are English.” “Is it that obvious?” “You apologized before I insulted you.” He closed the guidebook. “I’m Ben.” “Alessandra.” “Alessandra.” He attempted the pronunciation carefully. She tilted her head. “Not terrible. Very academic.” “I am an academic.” “I know. You have the face.” “What does that mean?” “Like you are always looking for footnotes.” She plucked the guidebook from his hand before he could object. The motion was so quick he assumed he had imagined it. “You have been here three days,” she said, scanning the pages. “Four.” “Worse. Four days and you are still reading about Rome instead of looking at it.” “I’m researching seventeenth-century civic ritual.” “You are researching boredom.” She snapped the book shut and tucked it beneath her arm. Ben blinked. “I’m sorry, that’s mine.” “Now it is a ticket.” “A ticket to what?” “Rome.” She kicked the motorcycle upright. “Get on.” “I beg your pardon?” “Do not beg. It makes you look English.” *** Ten minutes later, Ben was clinging to the back rail while Alessandra threaded through traffic with the confidence of someone who considered traffic a personal challenge. “Are you sure this is legal?” he called. “Absolutely not!” She laughed, leaned into a turn, and swept them past the Pantheon. Ben’s stomach remained somewhere near the Trevi Fountain. They stopped beside a narrow street where laundry sagged between ochre buildings. Alessandra parked beneath a sign that appeared to prohibit parking, stopping, standing, breathing, and perhaps thinking. Ben climbed off, pale. She watched him with interest. “You are not dead.” “I’m reassessing my life choices.” “Excellent. That is what Rome is for.” She led him through a side door into a courtyard fragrant with jasmine. A woman on a balcony shouted down at them. Alessandra shouted back, rapid-fire Italian. Ben looked from one to the other. “What did she say?” “She says I am shameless.” “And what did you say?” “That she is jealous.” The woman threw a dishcloth at them. Alessandra caught it, bowed, and returned it through the open window. As they left, Ben noticed a small brass key in Alessandra’s gloved hand. “Did that belong to the door?” She examined it as though surprised to find it there. “Maybe.” “Alessandra.” “What?” “You stole a key.” “I borrowed a key.” “Without asking.” “Then it is a very short-term loan.” She slipped it into her pocket and smiled at his horrified expression. “Relax, professore. I am a troublemaker, not a criminal.” “That distinction may be legally complicated.” “Good. You are waking up.” *** At midday she took him to a market near Campo de’ Fiori and ordered him to eat something he could not identify. “It has tentacles,” Ben said. “It has flavor.” “It’s looking at me.” “Then look back. Establish dominance.” He took a bite. Alessandra watched him chew. “Well?” “It’s surprisingly good.” She leaned closer. “You expected Rome to be made entirely of pasta?” “I expected lunch to be less confrontational.” “Your mistake is expecting things.” She stole a fig from a vendor’s tray as they passed. Ben caught her wrist. “You can’t do that.” She looked at his hand around her wrist, then at his face. For the first time all day, she went still. The market noise seemed to draw back: vendors calling, scooters coughing, a church bell striking twelve. “Can’t I?” she asked. Ben released her immediately. “I mean—you should pay.” Alessandra held his gaze for one suspended second, then tossed a coin onto the vendor’s table without looking. “There. Morality restored.” Her pulse beat beneath his fingers in his memory. *** In the afternoon she took him to a rooftop above Trastevere by a route involving two locked gates, a drainpipe, and Ben’s repeated declaration that he was not equipped for urban climbing. “You are a professor,” Alessandra said, hauling him over a wall. “You climb into other people’s ideas all day.” “I have never climbed a wall in tweed.” “You should publish on it.” The rooftop overlooked a maze of terracotta roofs. Rome glowed beyond them, grand and battered and impossible. Ben stood at the edge, breathless. Alessandra sat on a chimney pot and produced his guidebook. “You kept this,” he said. “I was deciding whether it deserved to live.” She handed it back. A postcard had appeared between the pages: a faded photograph of the Colosseum at night. “I didn’t have that before.” “No?” “No.” “Then Rome gave you a souvenir.” “You put it there.” “Can you prove it?” He smiled despite himself. “You’re a menace.” “A charming menace.” “I haven’t agreed to charming.” “You followed me onto a roof.” “That may have been temporary insanity.” “Same thing.” The wind lifted a strand of her hair. Ben wanted to touch it. Instead, he adjusted his spectacles. Alessandra noticed. Her smile softened, though only slightly. “You are very polite.” “I’m trying to be.” “Why?” He looked out over the city. “Perhaps I’ve been polite for so long I no longer know what I’m trying to avoid.” That surprised her. He saw it before she hid it. Then she nudged his knee with hers. “Careful, Ben Whitaker. You are becoming interesting.” *** At sunset, they returned to the Trevi Fountain. The crowd had thickened. Alessandra parked beside a row of scooters, her motorcycle’s colorful scar catching the orange light. Ben held up the guidebook. “You’ve ruined my itinerary.” “You had an itinerary?” “A very good one.” “Was it fun?” “No.” “Then I improved it.” She reached into his jacket pocket. He caught her hand this time. She looked down at their joined fingers. “You’re stealing from me now,” he said. “I was checking for valuables.” “And?” “Only one.” His heart gave an absurd, scholarly little stumble. Alessandra pulled free and stepped backward toward the motorcycle. “Tomorrow, professore.” “Tomorrow?” “If you survive the evening.” “What happens this evening?” She put on her helmet. “You go back to your hotel and wonder whether I exist.” “Do you?” She lowered the visor, but not before he saw her grin. The engine coughed awake. Ben stood in the fountain’s glittering spray, guidebook under his arm, the postcard hidden between its pages, and watched her disappear into Rome. Then he noticed something in his palm. A small brass key. On its ring, scratched in hurried letters, was an address. He looked toward the traffic where Alessandra had vanished. For once, Ben did not apologize to anyone before following.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-crafted piece that fulfills nearly every requirement of the prompt with style. The scene structure — Trevi Fountain, courtyard, market, rooftop, return to the fountain — gives the day a satisfying arc, and the escalating kleptomania (guidebook, dishcloth, key, postcard, fig) is handled with the requested subtlety: Alessandra never confesses it, and Ben's gradual recognition ("You stole a key." / "I borrowed a key.") tracks his slow loosening of propriety. The dialogue is the strongest element. It's sharp, character-differentiated, and consistently funny without tipping into sitcom rhythm. Alessandra's lines ("You apologized before I insulted you," "You are researching boredom") land as wit rather than quirk-delivery, and Ben's flustered formality is rendered through rhythm and diction rather than stated. The market wrist-grab moment is the best scene in the piece: it converts the comedy into genuine tension, gives Alessandra her first moment of stillness, and plants the ambiguity the prompt requested ("Can't I?"). Her enigmatic feelings are preserved right through the ending — the key with the address is a payoff that invites continuation without over-resolving. Weaknesses: the prose occasionally leans on a slightly mannered, fragmentary style ("Ben looked down. / Then up.") that flirts with gimmickry, though it mostly reads as deliberate rhythm. A few lines are a touch too pleased with themselves ("Rome was already making promises it had no intention of keeping" is a familiar kind of opener; "His heart gave an absurd, scholarly little stumble" is borderline cute). The rooftop exchange where Ben suddenly articulates his repression ("Perhaps I've been polite for so long...") is the one moment of slightly accelerated emotional confession, though it's brief enough to be forgivable and is immediately undercut by Alessandra's deflection. The "goat" line and "establish dominance" bit are mildly stock. Ben's transformation from timidity to following her into traffic is fast, but the story earns it through incremental steps — the wrist-grab, the pocket-catch — so it reads as escalation rather than unearned reversal. Character nuance is good: Alessandra is more than a manic pixie because her stillness at the market and her softening on the rooftop suggest interiority; Ben's politeness is given a psychological explanation without belaboring it. The ending's optimism is congruent with the material — a romantic beginning, not a resolution — so nothing feels falsely positive. Overall this is polished, professional, engaging work with only minor stylistic self-indulgences. + Cozy sci-fi: The Last Outpost — Score: 82.2
Prompt:
Cozy sci-fi The Last Outpost Nettle (or Nets to her friends) bartends at The Last Outpost -- a lazy hub for miners and merchants in an asteroid belt on the Andromeda outer rim. Escaping from her past life, Nets found a home here at the Outpost. They have, thus far, tolerated Net's flaws which she tries to keep in equilibrium with her assortment of talents. Her evenings involve chatting with patrons, negotiating the drama, intrigue, problems & love lives of the diverse crowd that filter through the Outpost. Tonight is no different, at least, until a frazzled looking stranger, tentacled dreads askew, quietly plops down at the bar: "Vega whisky, neat. Better make that a double." Write a chapter in this story. Establish conflict for narrative interest. Don't resolve the conflict within this chapter. Aim for about 60% dialogue. First person, present tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
### Chapter One: Double The glass breaks somewhere behind me, bright and sudden. Everyone in The Last Outpost pauses. Then the jukebox coughs back to life, a miner at table seven swears at his cards, and I turn toward the sound with my hand already reaching for the rag tucked through my belt. “Not mine,” calls Rusk from the kitchen. “Everything in the kitchen is yours when it breaks.” “Then charge the glass to me.” “I already charge you rent.” “That’s unrelated.” “It’s exactly related.” A few of the regulars laugh. The tension drains out of the room, leaving only the soft hum of the station’s life-support system and the low metallic shudder of docking clamps engaging three decks below. I find the broken tumbler beneath the service shelf. Nothing dramatic. Just a clean split through the middle, probably from one of the Outpost’s antique stabilizers failing again. I sweep the pieces into my palm and carry them toward the recycler. That’s when the stranger sits down. They move like someone trying not to be noticed and failing. Their tentacled dreads are askew, some coiled around their shoulders, others hanging limp against the high collar of their travel coat. Dust glitters along the seams. One of their lower eyes is swollen shut. “Vega whisky, neat,” they say. Their voice is soft, scraped raw. “Better make that a double.” I set the glass I’ve been polishing on the bar. “That bad?” The stranger looks at me with three eyes. The fourth is hidden under a curtain of silver-blue tentacles. “That depends.” “On?” “Whether you’re the sort of bartender who asks questions.” “I’m the sort who charges extra for them.” Their mouth twitches. Not quite a smile, but close enough to count. “Then I can afford several.” “Vega whisky is twelve credits.” “Put it on my tab.” I glance at their coat, their scuffed boots, the compact utility belt tucked beneath the fabric. “You have a tab?” “Not yet.” “Then you’re going to need a payment method.” They slide a small black wafer across the counter. It lands without a sound. I don’t touch it. The wafer is matte, with no station stamp, no merchant guild seal, no serial markings. Those things are designed to make people curious. This one is designed to make people disappear. “Cash is easier,” I say. “I don’t have cash.” “Then you’re having water.” Their tentacles twitch. “I was told The Last Outpost was discreet.” “People say lots of things about us. Most of them are untrue.” “Is that so?” “Someone once claimed our fried comet-eel was edible.” From the end of the bar, Juno raises a hand. “It is edible.” “It moved after you swallowed it.” “That was a medical issue.” “It was a lawsuit.” The stranger watches the exchange, gaze flicking from Juno to me. Something in their posture loosens. I tap the wafer with one finger. “What is it?” “A promise.” “Promises don’t cover drinks.” “This one does.” My instincts are not subtle. They put up a flare. They start shouting. They remind me that no one carrying a mystery wafer and a bruised eye comes to an asteroid bar for the ambiance. Still, I take it. The wafer is warm. Letters bloom across its surface. **AUTHORIZATION: PRIORITY TRANSIT** Beneath that, in smaller text: **VESSEL: ORISON** My fingers go cold. I turn the wafer facedown before the stranger can see that I recognize the name. “You know it,” they say. “I know a lot of ships.” “You know that one.” “Vega whisky?” “Please.” I pour two fingers into a glass and set it down. They lift it in both hands, inhale once, then drink half the measure without flinching. “That is not how you taste whisky,” I say. “I’m not tasting it.” “Then you’re wasting it.” “I’ve wasted better things.” A chair scrapes at table seven. The card game has gone quiet. I look up. Rusk is watching the stranger from the kitchen hatch. Juno has stopped pretending to organize the cutlery. Even the station’s old maintenance drone, Mallow, has rotated its camera toward the bar. The Last Outpost is a lazy place, but lazy does not mean blind. The stranger sets the glass down. “I need a room,” they say. “We don’t have rooms.” “You have the storage loft.” “We have a storage loft.” “I need it.” “Why?” “Because someone is looking for me.” There it is. The little spark dropped onto dry kindling. I lean on the bar. “Someone dangerous?” “Yes.” “Dangerous how?” “They have weapons.” “Everyone here has weapons.” “They have authorization.” The bar grows quieter. Outside the viewport, the asteroid belt turns slowly around us, all black stone and distant sunlight. Beyond it, Andromeda glimmers like spilled frost. I keep my voice low. “Station security?” “Compromised.” “Dockmaster?” “Compromised.” “Your charming personality?” “Exhausted.” “That one I believe.” They take another drink. Their hand trembles this time. I notice the blood beneath their sleeve. “You’re hurt.” “It’s not serious.” “People who say that are either lying or dead.” “I’m neither.” “Take off the coat.” “No.” “Then bleed on somebody else’s furniture.” Their eyes narrow. “You always this welcoming?” “Only with fugitives.” “I’m not a fugitive.” “Your transit authorization says otherwise.” The stranger goes still. I slide the wafer back across the bar. “Orison hasn’t been in this sector for six years.” “Seven.” “Worse.” “You knew the ship?” “I knew the name.” “That’s not what I asked.” “No, it isn’t.” For a moment, neither of us speaks. Then the Outpost doors hiss open. Cold station air rolls across the floor. Three figures enter in matching gray pressure coats, helmets tucked beneath their arms. Their boots are clean. Too clean for this side of the belt. The stranger’s tentacles coil tight around their neck. One of the newcomers scans the room. “Evening,” I call. The tallest one looks at me. “We’re looking for a passenger.” “Congratulations.” “An individual arrived here aboard the courier ship Orison.” “Lots of individuals arrive on ships.” “This one is wanted under intersystem emergency authority.” I polish the same already-clean glass. “Wanted for what?” The tall one’s gaze moves to the stranger. “Sabotage.” A murmur passes through the room. The stranger grips the whisky glass hard enough to make it creak. I set down my cloth. “You got a warrant?” The tall one smiles without warmth. “We have authority.” “That wasn’t my question.” “We can requisition this establishment.” “You can try.” Behind me, Juno quietly locks the kitchen hatch. Rusk reaches beneath the counter. Mallow’s camera iris narrows to a red pinprick. The stranger whispers, “You shouldn’t do this.” “I haven’t done anything.” “You’re about to.” “That depends.” “On what?” “Whether you’re actually a saboteur.” The tall officer steps toward the bar. The station lights flicker once. Somewhere in the walls, the Outpost groans, old metal shifting against old metal. I place one hand over the black wafer. “Tell me,” I say to the stranger, keeping my eyes on the officers, “what did you sabotage?” They look at me. Their answer is barely audible. “The thing that was keeping this station alive.” And beneath our feet, something enormous begins to wake.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong cozy sci-fi chapter that executes the prompt's requirements with notable skill. The first-person present-tense voice is consistent throughout, and the piece hits roughly the requested dialogue ratio. The opening with the broken glass is an efficient hook that establishes setting, tone, and supporting cast (Rusk, Juno) through banter rather than exposition. The worldbuilding is economical and effective: the wafer with "AUTHORIZATION: PRIORITY TRANSIT / VESSEL: ORISON," the antique stabilizers, the station's groaning metal. The bartender's voice is dry and wry ("I'm the sort who charges extra for them"), which suits the cozy genre while allowing genuine tension underneath. The conflict is well established and, per instructions, not resolved. The arrival of the gray-coated officers escalates stakes cleanly, and the final reveal — "The thing that was keeping this station alive" — reframes the stranger's guilt ambiguously: is she a saboteur or someone who disabled something dangerous? The closing line ("something enormous begins to wake") adds a hook without resolving anything. Weaknesses: The staccato single-line paragraph style, while punchy, becomes a tic over the length of the piece — nearly every exchange is broken into fragments, and the rhythm grows predictable. Some banter ("That's unrelated." / "It's exactly related.") is clever but borders on quippy-for-quippy's-sake. The bartender's instant recognition of the ship name, and her decision to shelter a stranger on that thin basis, is slightly convenient. The "compromised security / compromised dockmaster" beats are a touch stock. The stranger's characterization is thin — mostly mystery, little interiority — though that's defensible for a chapter one. The officers are generic antagonists. The ending's "something enormous begins to wake" is a familiar trope, though well deployed. Still, the prose is clean, the dialogue crisp, the tone coherent, and the cozy-tense balance is genuinely achieved. This is well above amateur work. + Young adult drama: Gone South — Score: 84.8
Prompt:
Young adult drama Gone South Taylor is a 16 year old teen with a history of "concerning behavioural patterns" (or that's how the stupid smug school counsellor worded it on the phone call to Mom). It shouldn't be a surprise: When you live in a backwater town in Tennessee, your choices are: a. be mind-fuckingly bored, or b. invent some drama. Two days ago, Taylor came out to their family as trans. This disclosure was *not* in the category of invented drama -- it was, in fact, the real deal, and a long time coming. It didn't go well. The last 48 hours had been pure disaster. In a moment of desperate inspiration, Taylor had decided to get the hell out of dodge. And so an escape plan was hatched and executed within the space of 30 minutes. That was last night. Now Taylor was two states away, having been unceremoniously ejected from their hitched ride in downtown New Orleans. Write the next chapter in Taylor's story as they find their feet in this new environment. Tell the chapter over the course of their first day in New Orleans, in which Taylor meets another runaway with issues and secrets. Taylor navigates this new world, not knowing who to trust or what the dangers are. Write in Taylor's voice, and incorporate their internal monologue as they grapple with intense & conflicting emotions. Also incorporate dialogue with the interesting characters Taylor meets. First person, mixed tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
### Chapter Two: No Map for This A saxophone is crying somewhere behind me. Not metaphorically. Not in the poetic, *New Orleans is full of sorrow and jazz* way the tourists probably tell it later, over cocktails they can pronounce. It’s a real saxophone, breathy and bright and slightly off-key, playing beneath the racket of traffic and voices and a woman shouting at somebody named Jerome. I keep walking. The pavement is hot through the soles of my sneakers. My backpack is cutting into my shoulder. I’ve been wearing the same black hoodie since yesterday, which is a terrible choice in Louisiana and an even worse choice when you’re trying not to look like a runaway. Unfortunately, my wardrobe at home consisted mostly of black hoodies and clothes my mother described as “deliberately hostile.” The street is packed. People drift around me in groups, laughing, carrying drinks in plastic cups, taking pictures of balconies and signs and each other. Everyone looks like they belong here. I look like a sixteen-year-old who got thrown out of a car. Which is technically what happened. “Good luck, kid,” the man had said, leaning across the passenger seat to open the door. As if he were giving me a lottery ticket instead of dumping me downtown. I’d stood there with my backpack and my last thirty-seven dollars while his truck disappeared into traffic. Then I’d thought, *Okay. This is the part where you become someone else.* That was six hours ago. So far I’m still me, only sweatier. My phone has one bar and three missed calls from Mom. I haven’t listened to the voicemail. I know what it will contain: anger, panic, maybe an attempt at tenderness that will make me feel worse than the yelling did. The saxophone changes songs. Something slow and ragged. I stop outside a closed souvenir shop and check the phone again. No new messages. My reflection stares back from the dark window: short hair, gray face, eyes too wide. A person trying very hard not to cry in public. “Hey.” I turn. The girl standing beside the doorway looks about eighteen, maybe nineteen. She has a shaved sidecut, a yellow dress under a denim jacket, and a bruise blooming purple beneath one eye. She’s holding a paper cup with no lid. “You lost?” she asks. “No.” She glances at my backpack. “You’ve been walking past here for ten minutes.” “I’m exploring.” “Sure.” The saxophone player launches into something faster. A couple dances badly in the street. The girl tilts her head. “You got somewhere to sleep?” I should keep walking. This is exactly the sort of person my mother warned me about, back when “people on the internet” were her primary source of information about the world. Strange city. Stranger girl. Bruise. No obvious job. “No,” I say. The girl’s expression changes, just slightly. “Name?” I hesitate. There are rules for being a runaway. I invented most of them on the drive down, while pretending to sleep. Rule one: Don’t tell anyone your real name. Rule two: Don’t get into another car. Rule three: Don’t trust anyone who says they can help. “Taylor,” I say, because it feels too late to lie about that. “Taylor what?” “Just Taylor.” She smiles without much humor. “Yeah. Same.” That should make me feel safer. It doesn’t. She takes a drink from the cup and winces. “I’m Miri.” “Miri what?” “Just Miri.” “Convenient.” “Very.” For a moment we stand there with the crowd streaming around us. She looks tired in a way that has nothing to do with sleep. There’s a thin white scar across her chin. Her fingernails are painted green, chipped down to the edges. “You’re not from here,” she says. “Tennessee.” “Thought so.” “Why?” “You keep looking up.” I look up automatically. Balconies spill over the street, decorated with flowers and lights. Somewhere above us, music thuds through an open window. Miri points down the block. “There’s a youth shelter near the edge of the Quarter. They don’t ask too many questions.” “Do they ask some questions?” “Probably.” “Like what?” “Whether you’re actually a kid.” “I am.” “Then you’re ahead of most of the people there.” She starts walking. I don’t follow immediately. The sensible thing would be to stay in a public place. Find a police officer. Call Mom. Go home. The sensible thing had been to wait until I was eighteen. But when I came out two days ago, Mom had stared at me like I’d handed her a live animal. Dad said, “This is a phase,” and then asked whether I’d been influenced by “that crowd.” My little brother watched from the stairs, silent and pale. The next morning, the school counselor called Mom and described my “concerning behavioural patterns.” I had laughed when she told me. Then I locked myself in the bathroom and packed. Miri glances back. “You coming?” I follow. We leave the busiest street behind. The noise thins, though the saxophone keeps threading through it all, fading and returning between buildings. My stomach twists. I haven’t eaten since a gas-station granola bar at dawn. Miri notices. “There’s a place up ahead. Cheap food.” “I don’t have much money.” “I didn’t ask.” “That’s not the same as saying you won’t.” She looks at me sideways. “You always this suspicious?” “Only when I’m awake.” That earns a real laugh. It surprises both of us. The restaurant is narrow and bright, with plastic menus taped to the windows. Miri orders fries and a bowl of something spicy. I get rice because it’s the cheapest thing. She pays before I can protest. “Consider it an investment,” she says. “In what?” “Making sure you don’t faint and become paperwork.” We sit in a booth beneath a television showing a baseball game with the sound off. My hands shake when the food arrives. I try to hide it, but Miri pushes the fries toward me. “Eat.” “I am.” “You’re interrogating the rice.” I eat. For several minutes, neither of us speaks. Outside, people move past the window in bright pieces: feathered hats, bare shoulders, cameras, glitter. New Orleans feels like it has swallowed every person who ever wanted to escape somewhere and given them a costume. Miri picks at her food. “So. What happened?” “Nothing.” “Right.” “I left home.” “Why?” I stare at the rice. The words have been trapped behind my teeth for two days. “I’m trans,” I say. Miri doesn’t flinch. Doesn’t ask whether I’m sure. Doesn’t say I’m too young. She simply nods. “That bad?” “My dad said I was trying to embarrass him.” “Mine said I was trying to kill him.” I look up. She’s watching the baseball game. “What did you do?” I ask. “Left.” “When?” “Three months ago.” “Where have you been?” “Here and there.” “That’s not an answer.” “It’s the one I’ve got.” There’s something underneath her voice. A locked door. Before I can ask, her phone buzzes on the table. She sees the screen and goes completely still. The bruise beneath her eye suddenly seems darker. “Who is it?” I ask. “No one.” The phone buzzes again. Miri grabs it and stands. “We should go.” “What? Why?” She’s already moving toward the door. I follow because I don’t know what else to do. Outside, the saxophone has stopped. The silence it leaves behind feels wrong. At the end of the block, a black sedan idles beside the curb. Miri sees it. So do I. A man in the driver’s seat turns his head. “Walk,” she says quietly. “Who is that?” “Walk, Taylor.” We move fast, not running. My pulse pounds in my throat. The sedan creeps forward beside us. Miri catches my wrist and pulls me into a crowded doorway. Her fingers are cold. The car rolls past. For a few seconds, neither of us breathes. Then she lets go. “You need to leave,” she says. “I thought you were taking me to a shelter.” “I was.” “Who was that?” “No one.” “Stop saying that.” Her face folds, anger and fear fighting for space. “You don’t know me.” “No, I don’t.” “And you shouldn’t trust me.” “I don’t.” “Good.” We stare at each other. Then Miri looks toward the street, toward the place where the car vanished. “Come on,” she says. “I know somewhere safer.” I should say no. Instead, I pick up my backpack. Because I am sixteen, homeless, hungry, and two states away from everyone who knows me. And because, for the first time since I left Tennessee, someone has looked at me and not asked me to become someone else.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-crafted continuation of Taylor's story. The first-person, mixed-tense voice is handled skillfully — present tense grounds the immediate New Orleans experience while past tense handles backstory (the coming out, the truck driver, the packing), exactly as instructed. The prose is lean and controlled, with a dry, sardonic teen voice ("You're interrogating the rice," "deliberately hostile" clothes) that stays consistent throughout. The New Orleans setting is vivid without tipping into postcard clichés — the off-key saxophone, the woman shouting at Jerome, the bright pieces moving past the restaurant window. The city feels alive and slightly menacing, appropriate to Taylor's disorientation. Miri is a strong secondary character: guarded, funny, clearly carrying her own secrets (the bruise, the phone, the sedan, "Mine said I was trying to kill him"). Her dialogue is clipped and natural, and the mirrored "just Miri"/"just Taylor" exchange is a nice touch of earned intimacy. The tension escalates believably — the sedan scene is genuinely tense, and Miri's abrupt shift from guide to warning ("You shouldn't trust me") lands well. Taylor's internal monologue captures conflicting emotions effectively: suspicion warring with hunger for acceptance, the invented "rules" of being a runaway, the memory of the family's rejection. The ending — Taylor following Miri anyway because she didn't ask Taylor to be someone else — is thematically resonant and earned, if slightly on-the-nose in its final explanatory lines. Minor criticisms: the ending's last two paragraphs spell out the emotional logic a bit too explicitly where the reader has already inferred it. Some beats (the bruised, mysterious older runaway) flirt with familiar territory, and the "No one." / "Stop saying that" exchange is a touch stock. The word count roughly matches the ~1000 word seed. The sedan threat is introduced and resolved quickly, though it functions as a hook rather than a plot hole. Overall this is polished, engaging YA writing with authentic voice and real emotional intelligence. My Apocalypse Buddy Write a wry, dry short story of survival and adventure loosely in the style of Terry Pratchett, set in the post-technological collapse world. [characters] - the animo-tronic stuffed koala, Chewy, from some long forgotten before time - midas, our hapless protagonist, who has a knack for finding himself in the worst kinds of trouble. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Midas and Chewy were deliberating over breakfast, which consisted of one boiled shoe leather and the last of the coffee-flavoured dust. “I’m saying,” said Midas, “that today we go out, find something useful, and come back before anything notices us.” Chewy sat on the table, animo-tronic eyes glowing with the stubborn cheerfulness of a device that had survived three centuries by refusing to acknowledge reality. “HELLO! I AM CHEWY!” he announced. “Yes,” said Midas. “You’ve been saying that since the batteries became archaeological.” Chewy’s left ear twitched. Somewhere inside him, a motor gave a dying whimper. Midas consulted the hand-drawn map. It showed their home base—the abandoned motorway toll booth they called Fort Nowhere—in the centre of a great deal of brown crayon. The surrounding landscape had once been a suburb. Now it was mostly thistle, rust, and the occasional chimney standing alone like a monument to indoor plumbing. “Our mission,” Midas continued, “is to find batteries, edible plants, and possibly a replacement for the bit of roof currently resting on your head.” “ADVENTURE!” said Chewy. “Let’s not use words that attract it.” The day’s first setback occurred before they had left the toll booth. Midas opened the door and was immediately bitten by a goat. The goat had no business being there. The motorway had been closed for eighty years, and the toll booth had no food. Nevertheless, it was a large goat with a severe expression and a clear sense of property law. Midas retreated, clutching his trouser leg. Chewy produced a pre-recorded sound of applause. After negotiations involving a tin of peaches, a shoelace, and Midas’s remaining dignity, the goat departed. It took the shoelace. They set out along the old service road. The road itself had split into three directions, all equally confident and all wrong. Midas chose the one with fewer bones. This turned out to be a mistake. The road led to an old supermarket, half-swallowed by ivy. The front doors were open, which was either promising or a warning. In the old world, people had considered such distinctions fussy. Inside, the aisles had been colonised by mushrooms. Chewy’s eyes illuminated a shelf of tins. “FOOD FOUND!” he cried. Midas picked up a can labelled PEACHES. “Excellent.” The can hissed. “Less excellent.” He put it down. A noise came from the back of the shop: a metallic clatter followed by what sounded like an elderly refrigerator clearing its throat. Midas and Chewy crouched behind a display of collapsed breakfast cereal. From the storeroom emerged three scavengers wearing bicycle helmets and carrying improvised spears. Their leader, a woman with a beard made of braided string, held up a can opener. “Who’s there?” she asked. Midas rose slowly. “Just passing through.” “Everyone says that. Nobody passes through. They arrive, steal things, and leave with the bits that aren’t nailed down.” “We’re looking for batteries.” The woman pointed at Chewy. “Your bear’s a battery.” “Koala,” said Midas. “Whatever. He’s got lights.” Chewy’s head rotated one hundred and eighty degrees. “PLEASE DO NOT DISASSEMBLE ME,” he said. The scavengers stared. Midas, who had previously believed this feature made Chewy safer, realised that the world had changed. The escape was complicated by Midas stepping on a packet of powdered soup. It burst beneath his boot, producing a cloud that blinded everyone and smelled faintly of ham. He and Chewy fled through the loading bay while the scavengers shouted threats involving several specific organs. Outside, they ran straight into a ditch. The ditch was not on the map. It had once been a drainage channel and was now deep enough to contain a small weather system. Midas landed in mud. Chewy landed in Midas. The koala’s right eye went out. “Are you all right?” Midas asked. “HELLO! I AM CHEWY!” “That’s a yes, then.” They climbed out on the far side, where the remains of a wall bore a message in bright blue paint: **WHEN THE CROWS FACE EAST, FOLLOW THE BROKEN MOON. THE WILD REMEMBERS. SHELTER BELOW THE ROOTS.** Beneath it was a crude drawing of a crescent moon, three crows, and what appeared to be a sandwich. Midas studied it. Chewy studied it with one illuminated eye. “Could be a hidden refuge,” said Midas. “COULD BE A SANDWICH.” “People don’t usually graffiti sandwiches.” “THEY SHOULD.” The message changed the mission. They were no longer merely seeking batteries. They were seeking the fabled refuge of the wilds, a place where survivors allegedly lived beneath the earth, possessed clean water, and had somehow preserved the concept of socks. The crows, unfortunately, were facing in every direction. Midas selected east by consulting the sun, a compass made from a needle, and the goat, which wandered past and looked judgmental. The goat appeared to favour the north. Midas went east. By noon they had crossed a field of waist-high nettles, one abandoned tennis court, and a bridge whose far end had fallen into a ravine. Chewy’s speaker began emitting fragments of nursery songs. Midas acquired three nettle stings, a sprained wrist, and a growing suspicion that the graffiti had been written by someone with a sense of humour. At last they found the broken moon: a concrete water tower with a crescent-shaped crack. Beneath it, tangled in the roots of a gigantic tree, was a metal hatch. Midas brushed away the leaves. A voice spoke from below. “Password?” Midas froze. Chewy’s remaining eye brightened. “HELLO! I AM CHEWY!” There was a pause. “Close enough,” said the voice. The hatch opened. A ladder descended into warm darkness. Midas looked at Chewy. “This might be salvation.” “ADVENTURE!” “It might be a trap.” “ADVENTURE!” “It might be both.” They climbed down. The refuge was a cellar containing six people, two goats, shelves of jars, a water pump, and a sign reading **NO HEROES, NO PROPHECIES, NO DISCUSSIONS ABOUT THE OLD WORLD AFTER SUNSET**. The bearded scavenger from the supermarket stood beside the pump. “You,” she said. Midas raised one hand. “In my defence, the soup was already unstable.” She sighed. “The refuge accepts travellers. It also accepts labour. You can stay if you repair the pump.” Midas looked at the pump. It was enormous, rusted, and leaking. Chewy leaned forward. “WARNING,” he said. “THIS OBJECT MAY BE A PUMP.” They spent the afternoon repairing it. Midas lost a fingernail, a sleeve, and the argument with a bolt. Chewy was used as a diagnostic instrument, a paperweight, and briefly as a hammer. When the pump finally coughed to life, it delivered three drops of water and a fish. Nobody knew where the fish came from. By sunset, Midas and Chewy began the journey home with a jar of water, two batteries, a replacement roof panel, and a goat following them at a suspicious distance. They returned to Fort Nowhere in multiple ways: Midas walked, Chewy was carried under one arm, the goat arrived by an unrelated route, and the roof panel came down from the sky when a hawk dropped it. They were worse for wear. Midas was limping, Chewy was missing an eye and making whale noises, and the goat had eaten the map. Still, they had survived, found a refuge, and acquired batteries. Midas opened the door. Inside, the roof collapsed. Chewy’s head rotated. “HOME SWEET HOME!” he said. Midas looked at the rubble. “Tomorrow,” he said, “we’re staying in.” The goat bit him again.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece delivers a competent Pratchett-adjacent comedy of post-apocalyptic survival. The dry, deadpan narration ("a large goat with a severe expression and a clear sense of property law") and Chewy's malfunctioning animo-tronic repetition ("HELLO! I AM CHEWY!") are the strongest comedic engines, and the running gags (the goat, the soup, the sandwich graffiti) mostly land. The structure follows the brief faithfully: deliberation over breakfast, a mission that goes sideways repeatedly (goat, scavengers, ditch, nettles), and a return "in multiple ways, worse for wear" — the story even winks at the prompt's odd phrasing, which is a nice touch. Weaknesses: the middle sags slightly with episodic setbacks that feel listed rather than escalating; the graffiti/refuge subplot is introduced and resolved too quickly to carry weight, making the refuge feel like a plot convenience rather than a discovery. The scavenger woman's reappearance at the refuge is convenient and under-motivated. Some jokes are telegraphed ("It might be both"). The prose is functional and witty but rarely rises to genuine elegance; imagery is sparse and mostly list-like. Characters are charming but thin — Midas's characterization is entirely "hapless," Chewy's entirely "broken toy," with little interiority or growth, though that's arguably the mode. The ending's roof collapse and final goat bite are well-earned lightness, and the piece wisely resists sentimentality. Dialogue is snappy and Pratchett-flavored, occasionally too quippy. Overall: a solid, funny, well-structured genre pastiche that stops short of brilliance. + Romance: Love in the Limelight — Score: 84.5
Prompt:
Romance: Love in the Limelight. Write one scene within a larger story set in Wales. A famous (fictional) actor ducks into a small-town bookstore to escape paparazzi. The scene takes us through the characters meeting in this odd circumstance. Over the course of the scene, the actor and the bookstore owner have a conversation charged by an undercurrent of unspoken chemistry. Write the actor as somewhat of a rogue with a fragile ego, which needs to be fed by having everyone like him. He is thoroughly charming, but the bookstore owner seems (at least superficially) immune to this; which paradoxically provokes a genuine attraction and derails the charm offensive. The bookstore owner, despite the superficial rebuffs of the actor's charm, is inwardly more than a little charmed and flustered despite themselves. Write primarily in dialogue, in the distinct voices of each character. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The bell above the door gave a thin, startled jangle. “Shut it,” said the man who came through it. Megan Price looked up from her ledger. “Good afternoon to you too.” “Please.” He pushed the door closed with both hands, then leaned against it as though he’d been running from a fire. Outside, beyond the rain-streaked window, two figures hurried past with cameras raised. Megan glanced at them, then at him. “Oh,” she said. The man removed a black baseball cap and shook rain from his hair. “That sounded ominous.” “You’re Rhys Llewelyn.” “I was hoping you’d say, ‘That sounded handsome.’” “I don’t think anyone’s ever said that.” He pressed a hand to his chest. “Cruel. I’ve only just met you.” “And yet you’ve already asked me to lie.” “Have I?” “You’re not here to buy a book.” “Not initially.” Megan closed the ledger. “The door is behind you.” “Those photographers are behind me.” “Then you’ve brought them.” “I rarely bring photographers anywhere. They’re very bad company.” “You’re an actor.” “Among other sins.” She looked past him. The paparazzi had stopped outside the café opposite, peering through the rain. One of them pointed at the bookshop. Rhys noticed. His expression changed—not dramatically, but the charm slipped half an inch, revealing something tight and young beneath it. “Could I stay five minutes?” he asked. Megan should have said no. The shop was small enough that his presence seemed to rearrange the air. He was taller than he appeared on posters, and wetter, and less polished. A dark coat, expensive boots, a faint cut on his cheek. He looked like trouble with excellent cheekbones. “Five minutes,” she said. “Don’t touch the first editions.” “I’m wounded you’d suspect me.” “You’re an actor. You make a living pretending to be other people.” “So do booksellers. ‘This is a wonderful novel, you must read it.’ Meanwhile, you’re thinking, ‘Please remove yourself from my premises.’” “I’m thinking that now.” He smiled. It was disarming. Megan hated that immediately. Rhys wandered toward the nearest shelf. “You own this place?” “Run it.” “Difference?” “The owner lives in Canada and thinks the internet is a fad.” “Ah. So you’re the one keeping civilisation alive.” “Civilisation has a loyalty card.” “May I have one?” “You have to buy something.” “I’m being persecuted.” “You’re hiding in a bookshop.” “Exactly. I’m a refugee.” “From what?” “Women with telephoto lenses. And one man who insists on asking whether I’m in love with my co-star.” “Are you?” “With my co-star?” “With anyone.” He turned, and the question landed more cleanly than she’d intended. “That’s a dangerous thing to ask a man in hiding.” “You can avoid answering. Actors do that professionally.” “Only when we’re sober.” Megan returned to her ledger, though the numbers had lost their shape. Rhys pulled a paperback from the shelf. “You have a section for Welsh writers.” “We are in Wales.” “Some people would say that’s no excuse.” “Some people are English.” “Some people are comedians.” “Some people are both.” His eyebrows lifted. “You’re not particularly impressed by me, are you?” “I’m sure you’re very impressive.” “That’s worse.” “Why?” “It sounds like something someone says after reading a parking notice.” Megan tried not to smile. “You’ll survive.” “I’m not certain. My ego is delicate.” “That must be difficult for everyone around you.” “It is. I require constant reassurance.” “Have you considered therapy?” “Several times. My therapist says I need to stop performing.” “And?” “I told her I’d think about it.” The bell gave another jangle as a gust shook the door. Rhys glanced toward the window. The photographers were still there. His fingers tightened around the book. Megan saw it. “They’ll get bored.” “They don’t.” “Then you should charge them rent.” “I’m serious.” “So am I.” He looked down at the paperback. “They make everything feel like a verdict.” The lightness had gone from his voice. Megan said, “You can leave through the back.” “I know.” “Then why aren’t you?” He swallowed. “Because if I go out there, I have to smile.” “That’s your job.” “No. My job is pretending to be terrified in front of a green screen. Smiling is… maintenance.” She studied him. “You’re afraid of being disliked.” His gaze flicked up. “That obvious?” “Only because you keep checking whether I am.” For once, he had no answer. Rain ticked against the glass. Somewhere in the back room, the ancient radiator clanked like a disapproving uncle. Rhys set the book down. “When I was seventeen, I auditioned for the youth theatre in Cardiff. I forgot every line. Not one—every line. Just stood there while three people watched me drown in silence.” Megan’s expression softened despite herself. “I got the part,” he continued. “They thought I was doing something subtle. I wasn’t. I was having a panic attack.” “What did you do?” “Went on stage every night and pretended I’d meant to look frightened.” He smiled faintly. “People said it was brilliant.” “And that was the beginning?” “That was the beginning of people liking me for being afraid.” Megan closed the ledger. “Perhaps they liked you because you were good.” “That’s a less interesting explanation.” “It’s probably the true one.” He looked at her as if she’d offered him something valuable and he didn’t know where to put it. Then the charm returned, but uncertainly now. “You know, most people ask for a photograph by this point.” “Most people have better manners.” “I can improve.” “Can you?” “I’m extraordinarily teachable.” “Name one thing you’ve learned.” He considered. “That the owner of Gorse Lane Books has green eyes.” Megan’s pen slipped from her fingers. Rhys blinked, apparently startled by his own honesty. “That wasn’t—” “It was a very poor attempt at charm.” “Yes.” “And you usually do better?” “Much better.” “Your ego must be devastated.” “It is. But you’re looking at me, so it’s recovering.” She bent to retrieve the pen, aware of the warmth rising in her face. “You’re impossible.” “I’ve been called worse by people who later apologised.” “Did they mean it?” “Usually.” The photographers moved outside. A camera flashed through the window. Rhys flinched. Without thinking, Megan stepped between him and the glass. He looked down at her. “You don’t have to do that.” “I know.” “Why did you?” “Because you’re blocking the Welsh poetry.” A reluctant laugh escaped him—real, rough-edged, and far more attractive than the practiced smile. The bell rang again as the back door opened in the hallway. Megan pointed. “There. Your escape route.” Rhys didn’t move. “Your five minutes are up.” “I know.” “Then go.” He glanced at the window, then back at her. “Will you be here tomorrow?” “It’s a bookshop.” “That wasn’t an answer.” “It was the only one you’re getting.” His smile steadied, though something in his eyes remained vulnerable. “I’ll come back for the book.” “You haven’t bought one.” “I’ll choose carefully.” “You’ll need to.” “Because you’ll judge me?” “Because I’ll be watching.” That stopped him. Megan regretted saying it. Rhys, naturally, did not. “Tomorrow,” he said. “Don’t be late.” He slipped through the back door. A moment later, the alley swallowed him. Megan stared at the empty doorway, then at the paperback he’d left on the counter. She picked it up. Inside the cover, written in black ink, was a phone number. And beneath it: *For emergencies involving photographers, fragile egos, or Welsh poetry.*
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong scene that hits the brief with notable precision. The dialogue-first construction is sustained throughout, with nearly the entire scene carried by exchanges between Rhys and Megan. The Welsh setting is lightly but adequately established (Welsh writers shelf, Cardiff youth theatre, Gorse Lane Books, rain). The actor is written as a charming rogue with a fragile ego—the panic attack origin story, the therapist joke, "I require constant reassurance" all serve this. Megan's superficial immunity masks inner flusterment, delivered mostly through physical tells (the dropped pen, warmth rising in her face, numbers losing their shape)—effective show-don't-show. The banter is genuinely sharp and witty. Lines like "Civilisation has a loyalty card," "That sounded ominous" / "I was hoping you'd say 'That sounded handsome,'" and "Because you're blocking the Welsh poetry" land well. The rhythm of short exchanges occasionally flirts with being too polished—every line is a quip, giving it a slightly overwritten, screenplay-polished quality where a bit of mess might feel more natural. Some exchanges (the "Some people are..." chain) flirt with cuteness. The emotional pivot to vulnerability (the "verdict" line, the Cardiff audition confession) is well-timed and gives the scene its necessary depth, though the confession itself is a touch well-worn as a device. The ending—him slipping out the back and leaving a phone number with a wry inscription—is charming and congruent with the tone. Megan stepping between him and the window flash is a nice unscripted gesture that quietly reveals her investment. No unearned transformation; the characters end the scene only slightly shifted, which is appropriate for a first meeting. Weaknesses: the relentless quippiness occasionally feels authorial rather than character-driven; both voices occasionally converge into the same dry register, making them distinguishable more by role than by distinct diction. The imagery is serviceable but sparse (radiator "like a disapproving uncle" is the standout). Prose is clean and efficient, never purple. The scene could risk feeling like a template of the "immune-to-charm love interest" trope, but the execution elevates it above stock. Overall: a polished, engaging, professionally-crafted scene that fulfills nearly every instruction with skill, held back slightly by an over-uniform wit and a familiar emotional arc.
