+ Whalepunk fantasy: The Morska Conspiracy — Score: 56.2
Prompt:
Whalepunk fantasy The Morska Conspiracy The Morska thieves guild experiences a sudden power vacuum as its leader was arrested in a raid in the early hours of the morning. Aya, a young woman born into aristocracy, has a keen interest in both the sciences and the arcane, having inherited her mother's gift for immateria magick (an outlawed practice for which her mother was, regrettably, hanged by the neck). Aya, bored with the world of aristocracy, has been spending her nights moonlighting with this very guild (masked, naturally). Leveraging her latent ability to summon dark entities from the immateria, she quickly rose through the ranks of the guild. Now, recognising the opportunity of the sudden power vacuum, Aya and her close companions Katra and Simeon, make a play for heart of the guild's claim to power: an ancient scythan artifact, under guard of spell and key in the depths of the guild hq. In contrast with the desperate chaos they had navigated thus far, the entrance to the underhold felt suddenly too quiet. Aya braces herself and reaches for the door. Write the next scene as the trio enter the underhold and find themselves confronted by none other than the guild leader herself, decidedly *un*-incarcerated, and in possession of both weapons and bodyguards. Paint a vivid picture of of the confrontation. Story beats: Aya is captured and unmasked. The trio are captured. Aya attempts to stall their demise by negotiating on her value as a hostage -- as she grapples with the inevitable consequences of her role in the guild being brought to light. Incorporate dialogue in the authentic voices of the characters. Do not write a fight scene. Lean into the gritty Victorian aesthetic with the dialogue & worldbuilding, as well as elements of gothic horror. In this world, men trust brass and oil and steel; magicka is feared and barely understood. Write in third person past tense, incorporating both Aya's internal monologue, and a heavy dialogue component. 1000 words.
Model Output:
The door opened without a hinge-creak. That was the first wrongness. The underhold lay beneath the Morska guildhouse, below the counting rooms, below the kitchens and the sweating dormitories where smugglers slept in shifts. Aya had expected locks, wards, perhaps the warm metallic hum of a pressure engine contrived by some dead Scythan genius. She had expected the stink of lamp oil and wet wool. Instead, there was silence. Not the ordinary silence of stone, either. This was a silence that seemed to listen. Katra entered first, pistol drawn low. Simeon followed with one hand on the brass cylinder strapped beneath his coat—a compact little contraption of gears and spring-loaded teeth which he insisted could “persuade” any lock in the known world. Aya came last, her black mask tight against her face, the immateria stirring faintly behind her eyes. The chamber beyond was vast and vaulted, ribbed with iron braces that vanished into darkness. Green lamps burned along the walls, their flames steady despite the absence of air. Chains hung from the ceiling. At the far end, behind a cage of black metal, rested the artifact. It was no larger than a man’s skull. A crooked sphere of pale stone sat upon a plinth, its surface engraved with signs that crawled when looked at directly. Scythan work. Ancient, forbidden, and very much alive. Around it stood six figures in long oilskin coats. The guild leader sat in a high-backed chair before the cage. Madam Morska had been described as many things: drowned, hanged, deported, devoured by a harbor beast. Aya had believed the last rumor, chiefly because it had been delivered by Morska herself over supper. But there she was. Her silver hair was braided close to her skull. A dark coat covered her broad shoulders, fastened with bone toggles. In one gloved hand she held a long-barrelled pistol of blackened steel. In the other, a hooked boarding axe rested lightly against the floor. Two brass automata stood behind her, tall and narrow, their torsos plated in riveted copper. Their eye-lenses glowed the dull orange of banked coals. Katra stopped. Simeon whispered, “That is unfortunate.” Morska smiled. “Good evening, little rats.” The door slammed behind them. Katra fired first. The shot cracked like a cannon in the enclosed chamber. One of the automata moved with impossible speed. Its arm rose; a brass shield unfolded from its wrist. The bullet struck and flattened. Morska did not flinch. Aya felt the immateria gather in her chest, black and cold as deep water. She could call something. A finger, perhaps. A mouth. A crawling shape with too many joints. She could let it spill through the seams of the world and tear the room open. But there were wards here. She felt them now: old spellwork sunk into the stone, braided with wire and salt. They pressed against her gift like a hand over a child’s mouth. “Drop it,” said Morska. Katra’s pistol vanished beneath the muzzle of a rifle held by one of the coat-clad guards. Simeon’s brass device clattered to the floor. He raised both hands. Aya did not move. Morska tilted her head. “You especially.” “I have no idea what you mean.” “Of course not. You have been robbing my warehouses for eight months while wearing that mask. I admire the theatricality.” Katra glanced toward Aya. It was a small glance, but it carried the weight of a falling building. Morska rose from her chair. “Take them.” The guards advanced. Aya reached for the immateria. Something seized her wrist. Not a hand. A band of cold iron flashed into being around her arm, its surface etched with tiny letters. Pain lanced through her shoulder. The presence behind her eyes recoiled, shrieking without sound. Aya staggered. Simeon swore. “Aya—” “Don’t,” she snapped. Too late. One guard struck him behind the knee. He fell hard, and another twisted his arms behind his back. Katra fought the ropes until a rifle butt kissed her temple. She went still, breathing through her teeth. Aya was forced against one of the iron pillars. A guard caught the ties of her mask. “No,” she said. Morska watched her with an expression that was almost pity. “That is the trouble with secrets,” the older woman said. “They become terribly fragile once someone has a hand on them.” The mask was pulled away. Cold air touched Aya’s face. For one brief, impossible moment, no one spoke. Then Katra said, very softly, “Lady Aya Vey.” Simeon’s face had gone pale. Morska’s smile disappeared. The guards tightened their grip. Aya felt the entire architecture of her life collapse inward: her father’s marble halls, her mother’s blackened scaffold, the polite society that would smile as it fed her to the law. The guild had been the one place where she could be no one. A shadow among shadows. Now the shadow had a name. Morska stepped close enough that Aya could smell rain and gun oil on her coat. “Well,” she murmured. “The Vey girl.” “My family has nothing to do with this.” “Your family has everything to do with this. Aristocrats do not come into my house to steal unless they are bored, desperate, or dangerous.” “I’m all three.” “That may be the first honest thing you’ve said.” Aya glanced toward the cage. The artifact pulsed faintly, and something within it answered the dark pressure of her blood. She could feel its attention. Like a buried eye opening. “If you kill me,” Aya said, “you lose more than a thief.” Morska raised one eyebrow. “I know the harbor accounts. I know which magistrates are buying protection. I know where the Watch stores confiscated magicka and who sells it back to the river districts. I know the names of every guild lieutenant who has been skimming from you.” “Do you?” “I do.” “And what would you call the thing you are doing now?” “Negotiation.” “I would call it begging.” Aya’s voice was steady. Her heart was not. Morska leaned on her axe. “You think your title makes you valuable?” “No. My usefulness does.” “Your usefulness ended when you were caught.” “Then why are you still listening?” That struck home. Morska’s gaze sharpened. Behind them, the harbor gave a distant groan. Fog pressed against the narrow windows high in the stone walls. The foghorn sounded once. The noise rolled through the underhold, deep and mournful. Morska turned her pistol slightly, not away from Aya but toward her companions. “Your friends,” she said. “Are they useful too?” Katra spat blood onto the floor. “Don’t flatter yourself. We’re not hers to bargain with.” Simeon, still on his knees, gave a weak shrug. “Speak for yourself. I’m tremendously valuable.” “Quiet,” Katra said. “I’m attempting to establish market conditions.” Aya almost laughed. It came out as a breath. Morska’s guards forced her down beside them. The iron band around her wrist burned whenever she thought too closely about the immateria. It knew her. It had been designed for people like her. People like her mother. “Listen to me,” Aya said. “The Watch believes you were taken to Blackwater Prison. If they learn you’re here, they’ll raid this place by dawn. If I disappear, they’ll search my family’s estate. They will find the guild through me.” Morska crouched before her. “And if I let you go?” “You don’t.” “Then what are you offering?” Aya swallowed. “A hostage. A bargaining piece. Keep me alive, and my family will pay to recover me.” “Your father?” “He would pay to prevent a scandal.” “Your father would pay to prevent inconvenience.” “Money is money.” Morska considered her. “And when he learns his daughter has been consorting with thieves? When he learns why your mother died?” The chamber seemed to contract. Aya’s fingers curled against the stone. Morska’s voice lowered. “Yes. I know about the immateria.” The second foghorn sounded. Aya’s stomach turned. The old shame rose like bile. Her mother’s hands bound behind her. The priest’s voice. The crowd refusing to look at the condemned woman’s face. “I can be more valuable alive,” Aya said. “Perhaps.” “Then keep me.” “I may.” Morska stood and looked toward the artifact. Its pale surface shifted beneath the green lamps. “But I have not decided whether you are a hostage,” she said, “or a key.” The third foghorn sounded beyond the walls. This time, something answered from inside the cage. And in the dark between heartbeats, Aya felt the artifact recognize her.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The response delivers the requested scene with strong competence: the trio enters the underhold, finds Morska free and armed, is captured, Aya is unmasked, and she negotiates her value as a hostage while grappling with exposure. The Victorian-gothic texture is well executed — foghorns, brass automata, oilskin coats, the scaffold memory of her mother. The prose is controlled, favoring short declarative lines that build tension effectively ("That was the first wrongness"). Strengths: The dialogue is largely sharp and character-distinct — Morska's dry menace ("I would call it begging"), Simeon's gallows humor ("I'm attempting to establish market conditions"), Katra's terse loyalty. The unmasking beat lands with genuine weight, and Aya's internal collapse into shame and calculation feels earned. The recurring foghorn motif and the artifact's final recognition of Aya give the scene a satisfying gothic close without resolving falsely. Weaknesses: The staccato one-line paragraph structure, while atmospheric, becomes a tic — the piece leans on it heavily, occasionally flattening moments that deserved fuller rendering. Katra firing first edges close to the "no fight scene" instruction, though it's brief and immediately suppressed, functioning more as a beat of desperation than combat. The negotiation, while competent, resolves a touch too smoothly — Morska's pivot from menace to consideration happens quickly, and Aya's leverage arrives conveniently. Some imagery is stock (green lamps, glowing coal eyes, "black and cold as deep water"). The ending's "artifact recognizes her" is a familiar trope, though well-placed. The piece shows rather than tells for the most part, maintains tonal consistency, and the emotional complexity — shame, fear, aristocratic boredom curdling into peril — is genuinely present rather than asserted. Gunpowder Rendezvous Spike Spiegel & Revy Write a story where Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop) and Revy (Black Lagoon) meet in a seedy bar after both being hired for the same bounty. Their mutual attraction is complicated by their trust issues and competitive instincts. Include drinking, gunplay, and unresolved sexual tension that culminates in a motel room standoff. **Spike Spiegel (Cowboy Bebop)** Spike is a laid-back bounty hunter with a dark past as a syndicate enforcer. He practices Jeet Kune Do and is exceptionally skilled with firearms. He's chronically broke, constantly hungry, and addicted to cigarettes. Despite his carefree attitude, he's haunted by his past and the woman he left behind. He has a prosthetic eye from a past injury that affects his depth perception. He's fatalistic to the extreme, often saying he's already died once. He values freedom above all else and dislikes attachments, though he secretly cares deeply for his crew. Famous quote: "Whatever happens, happens." **Revy/Rebecca Lee (Black Lagoon)** Revy is a Chinese-American dual-wielding gunslinger with unparalleled shooting skills. She's foul-mouthed, chain-smoking, and has severe anger management issues stemming from childhood abuse. She's known as "Two Hands" for her ability to accurately fire two pistols simultaneously. She drinks heavily and solves most problems with violence. Despite her hardened exterior, she has moments of vulnerability, particularly around Rock. She has a dragon tattoo covering her right arm and typically wears extremely short shorts and a black crop top regardless of the situation. Famous quote: "I'm not a good person, not a bad person. I'm just here." Third person, present tense. Length: 1000 words.

The neon jukebox plays the same scratchy rock track for the fourth time when Spike Spiegel walks into the bar. The song wheezes through its chorus, loses a speaker, and drags itself back to the beginning. Red light crawls over the bottles behind the counter. Blue light catches the smoke hovering beneath the ceiling. Spike pauses just inside the door, cigarette dangling from his mouth. The bar smells like spilled beer, gun oil, and old regret. Familiar territory. At the far end, a woman sits alone with two pistols on the table and a glass of whiskey between them. She wears black shorts, a cropped tank top, and an expression that suggests the furniture has personally offended her. A dragon coils down her right arm. She looks up. One hand moves toward a pistol. Spike smiles faintly. “You always greet strangers with a gun?” “Only the ones who look like trouble.” “Then I’m flattered.” “You look broke.” “That too.” The bartender sets down a glass without being asked. Spike slides onto the stool beside her, keeping his hands visible. The jukebox starts the song again. The woman’s eyes narrow. “You’re Spike Spiegel.” “Depends who’s asking.” “Rebecca Lee.” “Revy.” “People who like breathing call me Revy.” Spike glances at the pistols. “You must be the other bounty hunter.” “Funny. I was about to say the same thing.” Their target is Manny “Muzzle” Varga, a syndicate accountant who has stolen six million dollars and a data chip containing enough names to start a small war. The employer has offered one hundred thousand to whoever delivers him alive. Neither of them believes the alive part matters. Spike takes a drink. It is cheap bourbon pretending to be whiskey. Revy watches him swallow. “You working alone?” she asks. “Usually.” “Usually means no.” “Usually means I don’t answer questions from people with anger problems.” Revy laughs once. It has no humor in it. “You got a problem with anger?” “No. I have a problem with bullets.” “Then you’re in the wrong line of work.” Spike’s cigarette burns toward his fingers. He stubs it out and lights another from the ember. Revy lights hers with a silver lighter, leaning close enough that he catches the scent of smoke, liquor, and something warm beneath both. For a moment, neither looks away. Then Revy says, “You’ve got a dead-eye stare.” “Prosthetic.” “Didn’t ask.” “Most people do.” “I’m not most people.” “That’s what most people say.” The jukebox reaches the chorus again. Someone in the back throws a bottle at it. The bottle misses. The song continues. Revy drains her whiskey. “Varga’s at the Saint Lazarus Motel. Room twelve. I’m taking him.” Spike signals the bartender for another drink. “That’s a shame. I already made plans.” “With your hand?” “With the money.” Her mouth curls. “You think you can beat me to him?” “I think you can try.” The first gunshot comes from the bar’s entrance. A man in a gray coat fires at Revy. Spike moves before the muzzle flash finishes blooming. He drops beneath the bar as the bullet tears through the wall behind him. Revy kicks the table over, draws both pistols, and fires from the floor. Two shots. Two men outside stagger backward. Spike rolls, catches a shooter by the wrist, and drives an elbow into his throat. His depth perception slips for half a heartbeat; the room doubles, then snaps together. He compensates, twists, and sends the man through a chair. The bar explodes into motion. Revy fires one-handed over the overturned table, laughing as glass rains down. “You always bring this many friends?” “Not mine.” “Could’ve fooled me!” Spike ducks behind the counter. He fires once through a hanging shelf. A gunman drops behind it. The scratchy song continues, absurdly cheerful. Revy rises, both pistols flashing. Her aim is perfect, brutal, effortless. When the last attacker falls, she stands amid smoke and broken bottles, chest lifting beneath her black top. Spike emerges with a fresh cigarette between his lips. She looks him over. “You’re slow.” “You’re loud.” “You’re still alive.” “Whatever happens, happens.” That earns him a strange look—half irritation, half interest. They leave before the police arrive. Outside, rain needles the pavement. Revy steals a cigarette from his pack without asking. Spike lets her. They walk beneath the motel’s failing neon sign, close enough for their shoulders to brush. “Why’d you save me?” she asks. “Didn’t.” “You pulled a guy off my back.” “He was in my way.” “Bullshit.” “Usually.” Room twelve has one bed, one chair, and a bathroom door that refuses to close. Varga is inside, bound to the chair, bleeding from the mouth. He looks from Spike to Revy and starts laughing. “Two hunters,” he says. “That’s unfortunate.” “For you,” Revy replies. Varga reaches for the data chip concealed beneath his tongue. Spike catches his jaw. Revy presses a pistol beneath his chin. They work together for exactly three seconds before turning their guns on each other. Spike’s pistol points at her chest. Both of Revy’s point at his heart. Varga stops laughing. Rain ticks against the window. The jukebox melody still seems to echo in Spike’s head. “You’re not taking him,” Revy says. “Neither are you.” “I shoot you, I get paid.” “Maybe. But you’ll have to explain the missing chip.” “I’ll shoot him too.” “Then we’re both out of luck.” Her eyes flick to his prosthetic eye, then back to the real one. “You always this calm when someone’s aiming at you?” “I’ve been dead once already.” “Cute.” “Wasn’t a joke.” Something shifts in her face. Not softness. Revy does not do softness. But recognition, perhaps—the ugly understanding of someone who has survived by pretending survival means nothing. “You got ghosts?” she asks. “Whole cemetery.” “Same.” The distance between them feels smaller than the room. Spike lowers his gun by an inch. Revy’s fingers tighten around her grips. “Don’t.” “Don’t what?” “Look at me like that.” “Like what?” “Like you’re trying to figure out if I’m worth the trouble.” Spike studies her. “I already figured it out.” Her breath catches. The anger returns to cover it. Then Varga moves. Revy fires first—not at Spike, but at the ceiling. Spike spins and shoots the chain holding the motel’s ancient light fixture. It crashes down between them and Varga. In the confusion, Revy grabs the chip. Spike catches her wrist. For one suspended second, they stand almost touching, guns trapped between their bodies. Her dragon tattoo brushes his sleeve. His cigarette drops to the carpet and burns unnoticed. “Let go,” she says. “Not yet.” “I’m gonna count to three.” “You only need two.” Her eyes flash. She head-butts him. Spike stumbles, laughing despite the blood blooming at his nose. Revy bolts through the bathroom door. He follows, but she has already climbed through the window onto the fire escape. She looks back over her shoulder. “Next time, Spiegel.” “Next time, Revy.” “Bring more money.” “Bring fewer bullets.” She smiles like a threat and disappears into the rain. Inside, Varga groans. The room smells of gunpowder and smoke. Spike retrieves his cigarette, relights it, and stares at the open window. The job is ruined. The bounty is gone. His head hurts. He exhales slowly. Whatever happens, happens. Outside, two gunshots crack through the night—warning shots, perhaps. Or an invitation.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece delivers a competent noir pastiche with strong genre instincts. The prose is lean and rhythmic, using short declarative sentences and staccato dialogue exchanges that suit both source materials. The bar scene establishes atmosphere efficiently—jukebox repetition, red and blue light, smoke—and the gunfight is choreographed with clarity. Character voices are largely faithful: Spike's fatalism ("I've been dead once already"), Revy's profanity-adjacent aggression and vulnerability-avoidance, and the mutual recognition of "ghosts" all land believably. Strengths: the banter is punchy and in-character; the motel standoff fulfills the prompt's requirements; the ending preserves both characters' independence without forcing a romance, which is the right call for these two. The "invitation" closing gunshots are a nice ambiguous beat. Weaknesses: the dialogue occasionally becomes a machine of interchangeable quips—"Didn't ask." / "Most people do." / "I'm not most people." / "That's what most people say"—which is clever but hollow, trading character voice for rhythm. The Varga subplot is thin; he exists purely as a MacGuffin and his "Two hunters. That's unfortunate" line is functional at best. The emotional turn ("Something shifts in her face... recognition") is told rather than shown, and the attraction is asserted through proximity rather than earned tension. Some imagery is stock ("smoke, liquor, and something warm beneath both"). The head-butt escape resolves the standoff a bit too neatly. The piece is stylish but somewhat surface-level—competent genre execution without a distinctive perspective of its own. + Folk horror: Útiseta — Score: 84.1
Prompt:
Folk Horror: Útiseta Write a chapter set in rural northern Sweden in the mid-1990s. Linnea, a teenage girl from Stockholm, has reluctantly moved to a small village with her parents after her father's job transfer. She's befriended Astrid, a local girl who claims her grandmother taught her ancient practices passed down through generations. Astrid has been introducing Linnea to "midnight games" that involve old rituals, convincing her they can use them to learn classmates' secrets or influence their behavior. Tonight, Astrid has convinced Linnea to participate in Útiseta—sitting out on an ancient burial mound at midnight to "receive knowledge from beyond." The chapter focuses on this single midnight excursion, the ritualistic preparations, Astrid's matter-of-fact instructions that mix teenage rebellion with eerily specific traditional elements, and the mounting tension as Linnea becomes increasingly uncertain whether they're simply scaring themselves or if something is actually responding to their presence. The narrative should maintain ambiguity about whether the strange occurrences are supernatural or psychological, while establishing the dangerous line they're crossing by treating ancient practices as entertainment. First person, past tense, told as Linnea's recollection of events in the present day (though this device should be largely transparent). 1000 words. Length: 1000 words.
Model Output:
I remember the gloves first. Astrid laid them on the kitchen table as if they were important instruments: two pairs of gray wool mittens, one patched at the thumb, and beside them a coil of red thread. “It’s below freezing,” I said. “It’s October.” “In Stockholm, October means rain.” “In Norrbotten, it means frost.” She pushed the mittens toward me. “Put these on before we leave. You can’t tie knots with numb fingers.” My parents were upstairs, arguing in low voices about the telephone bill. We had moved north three weeks earlier, and already their voices had acquired the careful, muffled quality of people who regretted being overheard. The house still smelled of cardboard and pine cleaner. Outside, the village had vanished beneath darkness, except for a few windows glowing across the road. “What are the knots for?” Astrid looked pleased that I’d asked. “Keeping things out.” “What things?” “That depends what comes.” She said it matter-of-factly, as if we were discussing mosquitoes. I put on the mittens. We left through the back door. Astrid carried a small canvas bag, and I carried the flashlight, though she told me not to use it unless she gave permission. The cold made the snowless ground crackle under our boots. Above the roofs, the sky was immense and black, scattered with stars I had never seen from Stockholm. The burial mound lay beyond the last houses, in a field that sloped toward the river. In daylight it looked like a low, grassy hump surrounded by birch trees. Astrid said there were several mounds, but only this one was “awake.” “You’ve done it before?” I asked. “Not alone.” “With your grandmother?” “Once. I was nine.” “And what happened?” “She told me not to ask questions until I knew how to listen.” That was the sort of answer Astrid had begun giving me since we became friends. She had a way of making ordinary words sound inherited. Her grandmother lived in a red house at the edge of the village and had once told Astrid that people in the north had always known how to speak with the dead. Not in church, Astrid explained, but in older ways: sitting out, listening at crossroads, leaving offerings where the land remembered. She called the games midnight games. We had already tried one with a bowl of water and three names written on scraps of paper. Another involved turning a key in a locked room while asking who was thinking of you. Astrid claimed they had made our classmate Mattias confess to stealing cigarettes. I thought Mattias had confessed because he was frightened of his father. Astrid said fear was only one kind of answer. At the mound, she told me to circle it three times without speaking. The grass was stiff with frost. The mound rose higher than I remembered, its crown silvered by moonlight. At the top stood a flat stone, half buried and furred with lichen. Astrid opened the bag. Inside were a candle in a saucer, a heel of rye bread, a little flask, and the red thread. “What’s in the flask?” “Water from my grandmother’s well.” “Why water?” “Because we’re asking for knowledge, not favors.” She placed the candle on the stone but did not light it. Then she tied one end of the thread around my left wrist and the other around hers. “So we don’t lose each other,” she said. “Lose each other where?” “In the dark.” I laughed, but she didn’t. We sat side by side on the mound, facing north. Astrid instructed me to put my hands flat on my knees, keep my feet planted, and breathe through my nose. She said I must not speak first, whatever I heard. If I felt someone sit behind us, I was not to turn around. “Why not?” “Because if it’s only wind, you’ll be embarrassed. If it isn’t, you’ll invite it closer.” The field was utterly still. Far away, a dog barked once and stopped. The village lights seemed smaller than they should have been. Astrid lit the candle. The flame leaned toward us, though there was no wind. “Ask silently,” she whispered, “what you want to know.” I thought of Stockholm. I thought of my old friends, who had stopped writing after my third letter. I thought of whether my father would lose his job again, whether my mother would decide she hated the north, whether I would ever stop feeling like a guest in my own life. Then I thought, unwillingly, of a question I had not told Astrid: Did they talk about me at school? The candle guttered. Something moved among the birches. I gripped the thread. “Did you—” “Don’t speak.” It could have been a branch. There was hardly any wind, but the trees shifted in separate, uncertain motions. One pale trunk bent, straightened, and bent again. Astrid began reciting under her breath. I recognized none of the words. They sounded Swedish at first, then older than Swedish, full of hard consonants and stretched vowels. Her grandmother’s language, perhaps, or something invented for the occasion. The thread between us tightened. I stared at it. Astrid had not moved, yet the red cord pulled taut as if someone had taken hold of it from the darkness between us. Her face had lost its smugness. Behind my shoulder, the snow—or frost, or grass—made a soft compressing sound. Someone sitting down. I remembered her warning and kept facing forward. My heart beat so violently that the mound seemed to pulse beneath us. Astrid’s fingers closed over mine. They were cold and shaking. The presence behind us breathed. At least, that was what I thought. A long, patient exhalation stirred the hair at my neck. I smelled wet earth, then smoke, then something sweet and rotten. The candle went out. In the dark, a bell chimed. Once. It came from the village church, though the church was nearly two kilometers away and no service was scheduled. The sound crossed the field cleanly, a single bronze note that seemed to hang above us long after it ended. Astrid whispered, “Don’t answer.” “I wasn’t going to.” “Not you.” The thread snapped. I turned. There was nothing behind us. Only the slope of the mound, the birches, and the black field beyond. Astrid was on her feet, dragging me upright. Her mittened hand crushed mine. We ran without collecting anything. The flask fell somewhere behind us. The candle remained on the stone, unlit, but when I glanced back I saw a small glow at the mound’s crown. It might have been the flashlight beam bouncing off frost. It might have been a flame. At the edge of the village, Astrid stopped. Neither of us spoke until the church bell’s echo had disappeared completely. “Your question,” she said. “What about it?” “Did you get an answer?” I wanted to tell her no. I wanted to say we had frightened ourselves in a field, that the thread had caught on a stone, that the bell had been rung by some late-night fool. Instead I looked down at my left wrist. The red thread was still tied there. Around it, in the frost-white skin, were four dark fingerprints.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a strong piece of folk horror that fulfills nearly all the prompt's requirements. The first-person past-tense recollection frame is established lightly ("I remember the gloves first") and remains transparent, as requested. The rural Norrbotten setting in the mid-1990s is convincingly evoked through small details: the telephone bill argument, the cardboard-and-pine-cleaner smell of the new house, the two-kilometer distance to the church. Astrid's matter-of-fact mixing of teenage bossiness with eerily specific traditional elements (knots "for keeping things out," well water "because we're asking for knowledge, not favors," the warning not to speak first) is exactly the register the prompt asked for, and it's the story's greatest strength. The ambiguity is well maintained: every supernatural event has a plausible mundane counter-explanation (branch, thread caught on a stone, flashlight on frost), until the final image of the fingerprints, which tips the scale just enough to be chilling without resolving the ambiguity entirely. The prose is clean, restrained, and controlled. Short declarative sentences build tension effectively ("The thread snapped." "I turned."). The dialogue is excellent — clipped, natural, and character-revealing; Astrid's lines ("If it's only wind, you'll be embarrassed. If it isn't, you'll invite it closer") carry inherited menace without overwriting. Linnea's interiority — the unanswered letters, feeling "like a guest in my own life," the secret question about classmates — grounds the horror in adolescent vulnerability, which is precisely the "dangerous line" the prompt requested. Minor criticisms: the word count is somewhat under the 1000-word target (roughly 850-900), a mild adherence issue. The "midnight games" backstory is delivered in a slightly expository block, though it's brief. The bell and the breathing presence are familiar folk-horror beats, and the fingerprints ending, while effective, is a well-worn trope. The mother and father are thin, though they're appropriately peripheral. None of these flaws seriously damage the piece; the pacing is tight, the escalation well-judged, and the ending earns its darkness through the accumulated restraint of everything before it. + Physical-spatial: Therapeutic Boundaries — Score: 80.7
Prompt:
**"Therapeutic Boundaries"** Write a first-person narrative from the perspective of a former professional athlete undergoing mandatory physical therapy after a career-destroying injury, harboring resentment toward recovery itself. Their physiotherapist is not only unnervingly attractive but also a former training partner from their competitive days who has successfully transitioned to a new career while the protagonist's identity remains shattered. We'll lean into the sexual tension of the scene by having her be attracted to him, but both of them attempting to maintain mental distance while being in physical contact as he shows her stretches & movements & manipulates her body, navigating the thresholds of pain. This scene MUST maintain complete physical coherence—every movement, stretch, and manipulation must be anatomically precise and spatially consistent. Paint an exceptionally vivid sensory picture through detailed attention to pain thresholds, involuntary responses to touch. Capture the suppressed, flaring tension of physical proximity, touch, and the controlled infliction of uncomfortable movements. Physical clarity is essential — readers must understand exactly what is happening with the body during each therapeutic technique. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I was good at knowing exactly where my body ended and the world began. On the track, that boundary had been useful. I could feel the lane beneath my spikes, the angle of my knee, the fraction of a second between strain and failure. After the injury, the boundary blurred. My right leg belonged to no one. It dragged when I told it to lift, trembled when I told it to hold, and burned with a private, vindictive intelligence. The physiotherapy room smelled of disinfectant, rubber, and the faint medicinal heat of the ultrasound machine. A wall-mounted diagram of the human musculature loomed over the treatment table, its painted tendons and red muscle bellies stretched into a permanent scream. Mara stood beside it with a clipboard. Former training partner. Current physiotherapist. Successful enough to have a degree, a clinic, and a life that had continued in a straight line. I had a brace, a ruined contract, and a knee that had decided my career was over before I did. “Lie on your back,” she said. “You always did enjoy giving orders.” “I always did enjoy watching you ignore them.” Her mouth tilted, but her attention stayed on my leg. That was the problem with Mara: she could make professionalism feel like a dare. I lay back. The table paper crackled beneath my shoulders. My right knee was supported by a foam bolster, leaving the joint slightly flexed. The incision along the front of the knee had healed, but the skin around it remained tight and hypersensitive. I could feel the room’s cool air across it. Mara pulled a stool to my right side. “We’re working on extension first. Your quadriceps are guarding.” “They’re protecting the joint.” “They’re protecting your fear of the joint.” I looked at the diagram. The printed quadriceps seemed to glare down at me. She placed one hand beneath my heel and the other lightly above my kneecap, not pressing on it, only stabilizing the thigh. “Let the leg go heavy.” “It is heavy.” “It’s resisting.” Her fingers were warm. That was all. Warmth, pressure, contact. I catalogued each sensation because cataloguing was safer than reacting. She lifted my lower leg a few centimeters, sliding the bolster away, then lowered the heel onto the table. The knee settled toward straight. At first there was only tension behind it, a cord drawing tight through the hamstrings. Then the joint reached its limit. Pain rose sharply, bright and clean. My quadriceps contracted without permission. Mara felt it. “Don’t fight the contraction.” “I’m not.” “You are.” Her thumb shifted to the inside of my thigh, near the vastus medialis, and her palm steadied the femur. She did not force the knee lower. She waited. The pain spread from the joint line into the back of my knee and down the calf. My heel pressed into the table. My breath shortened. “Red, yellow, or green?” she asked. “Yellow.” “Good. Stay there.” The instruction was infuriatingly calm. Her face was close enough that I could see the faint crease between her brows. She had always focused like that during training, as though the body in front of her were a puzzle worth solving. My body had once been worth something. She maintained the position for twenty seconds, then bent my knee by sliding one hand under my heel and guiding it toward my hip. The heel moved along the table; she did not lift the leg. My knee flexed gradually, the scar pulling at the front of the joint. At roughly ninety degrees, the resistance changed. The pain became denser, less sharp. My thigh muscles fluttered under her other hand. “Involuntary guarding,” she said. “I know what it is.” “I know you do.” Her hand remained on my thigh. The contact was clinical. My awareness of it was not. She eased the heel back out until the leg was nearly straight again, then released it. My foot fell a few centimeters and stopped against the table. “Your turn,” she said. “Heel slides. Ten.” I bent the knee, dragging the heel toward me. The movement was ugly and uneven. My pelvis shifted despite my effort to keep it still. “Keep the hip quiet.” “You could try being less attractive when you say that.” The silence that followed was immediate and complete. Mara’s gaze lifted to mine. Something flared there—brief, unwilling, unmistakable—before discipline closed over it. “That,” she said, “is exactly why we keep the hip quiet.” I laughed once, without humor, and continued. On the sixth repetition, the front of my knee began to burn. On the eighth, my hamstrings seized. Mara placed two fingers against the side of my pelvis, not restraining me, simply marking the motion. “Don’t compensate.” “I’m not compensating. I’m surviving.” “You don’t have to make every exercise a referendum on your career.” The words struck harder than her hands had. She moved to the side of the table and helped me sit up. My right leg hung cautiously, knee bent. The room tilted for a moment. Mara steadied my shin with one hand and my elbow with the other. The contact was brief, practical. My body still registered every point of it. “Stand with the crutches,” she said. I planted my left foot, then brought the right forward without bearing weight. The leg felt detached below the knee. Mara stood in front of me, close enough to catch me if I fell. “Weight shift. Left to right, only as far as comfortable.” “I can do it.” “I didn’t ask if you could do it. I asked you to do it correctly.” I shifted. The floor came up through my left foot. My right knee trembled, and pain flashed beneath the kneecap. Mara’s hand closed around my waist—not my hip, not my chest, but the narrow band above the pelvis where she could stabilize my center without pulling me toward her. My breath caught. Her eyes flicked to my face. She felt that too. “Yellow?” she asked. “Yellow.” “Then hold.” We stood there, balanced in the narrow space between pain and panic, her hand firm at my waist and my injured leg barely touching the floor. On the wall, the painted muscles remained frozen in their impossible certainty. Mara counted to five, then stepped away. The loss of contact was almost as noticeable as the contact itself. “Again,” she said. I hated her for saying it. I hated myself more for wanting her to put her hand back.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This piece is a strong execution of a demanding prompt. The physical therapy sequence is anatomically coherent: the bolster placement, heel slides, guarding responses, weight-shift exercises, and the therapist's hand positions (under the heel, stabilizing the femur, at the waist above the pelvis) are all spatially precise and clinically plausible. The "red, yellow, green" pain-scale device is a smart, authentic touch that also functions as a metaphor for the characters' emotional thresholds. The prose is controlled and lean, favoring short declarative sentences that mirror the protagonist's habit of "cataloguing" sensation to avoid feeling it. This creates a consistent voice: clipped, defensive, precise. The tension between Mara and the narrator is handled with restraint—her flared glance after his flirtatious remark, the "loss of contact" being as noticeable as contact itself. The dialogue is sharp and economical, with the "referendum on your career" line landing as the emotional pivot. Weaknesses: the piece is somewhat one-note in its emotional register—resentment and suppressed attraction are sustained without much modulation, and the ending, while thematically apt ("I hated myself more for wanting her to put her hand back"), is a fairly predictable beat. The muscular diagram "screaming" and "impossible certainty" imagery is slightly overworked. The backstory (career-destroying injury, ruined contract) is sketched thinly, though adequately for the word limit. Some metaphors ("private, vindictive intelligence") flirt with overreach but mostly stay controlled. The narrative is essentially a single scene with no arc beyond incremental physical progress, which is appropriate but limits depth. Overall, this is confident, professional work with excellent physical clarity and genuine tension, held back slightly by predictability and a narrow emotional range. + Historical fiction: High Seas and Low Vices — Score: 57.5
Prompt:
High Seas and Low Vices: British Naval Officer in the Opium Trade Character: Lieutenant James Merrick, a high-ranking officer in the British Royal Navy stationed in Canton, China in the 1830s. Once promising and decorated, now struggling with a severe opium addiction he hides from his superiors. Synopsis: Write a chapter following Lieutenant Merrick during a single day as he shirks his official naval duties in what has become a daily need to satiate the dragon. Told primarily in dialogue with the characters he interacts with. Focus on brief slices of his journey through the shadowy underworld of Canton: interactions with acquaintances, negotiations with local dealers, schemes and unsavoury jobs taken to fund his habit. Writing Task: Use rich sensory details to describe a day in the life of James Merrick. Write for a real sense of time & place while avoiding cliche. First person, past tense. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I woke to the rattle of rain against the shutters and the sour taste of yesterday’s smoke in my mouth. “Lieutenant?” The voice came from the passage. I opened one eye. Through the mosquito net, the room was a grey box: damp plaster, a washbasin filmed with oil, my uniform coat hanging from the peg like an accusation. “Go away, Chen.” “You told me to wake you before the tide turned.” “I tell everyone too much.” Chen pushed the door open with his shoulder. He carried tea in a blue cup and wore the same brown jacket he had worn for three years, though the cuffs had gone dark with use. “Your boat waits,” he said. “My boat may wait until the Empire collapses.” “Then it will wait longer than the boatman wishes.” He set the cup down. I reached for it, but my hand trembled so badly that the tea struck the saucer. Chen watched me. He watched everything. “Breakfast,” he said. “I have no appetite.” “You have no money, either.” At that, I sat up. The trembling had begun in my fingers and spread inward, a fine electric buzzing beneath the skin. I put my hand into my pocket and closed it around the jade figurine. It was a little seated Buddha, no larger than my thumb, smooth from years of anxious handling. My father had bought it in Macao when I was a midshipman and still believed discipline could govern a man’s appetites. I rubbed the jade with my thumb until its coolness steadied me. “How much?” I asked. “For tea?” “For what I owe.” Chen looked toward the shutters. Beyond them, Canton was waking in layers: boatmen calling on the river, wooden shutters banging open, the wet clatter of wheels over stone. Somewhere below, someone was frying garlic and river fish. The smell entered through the cracks and mingled with mildew, coal smoke, and my own sour sweat. “You owe the house for three nights,” Chen said. “You owe the boatman. You owe me.” “And I am an officer of His Britannic Majesty’s Navy.” “You are also thirsty.” I swung my legs from the bed. My boots were beneath it, still caked with mud from yesterday. “Find me work.” Chen gave a small laugh. “Work is what you have been avoiding.” “Then find me profitable avoidance.” He studied me for a moment. “There is a warehouse near the creek. A foreign merchant wants a letter carried to the Portuguese quarter. No questions.” “What is in the letter?” “If you ask, he will find someone else.” “How much?” “Enough for one pipe.” I rose too quickly. The room tilted. I gripped the bedpost and pressed the jade hard into my palm. Chen’s expression changed, but only slightly. “Two pipes,” I said. “One.” “Then I shall carry two letters.” He sighed. “You bargain like a fishmonger.” “I was trained by the Admiralty.” “Then the Admiralty has much to answer for.” By the time I reached the street, the rain had thinned to a warm mist. Canton pressed close on every side. Shop fronts leaned above the lanes, their painted signs dripping vermilion down the walls. A boy carrying baskets of greens slipped past me, shouting at a sedan chair. Two Sikh watchmen stood beneath an awning, their turbans bright against the wet morning, while a cluster of foreign sailors argued over a dice game beside a shuttered tavern. I kept my head down. “Lieutenant Merrick.” I stopped. Mr. Vale stood beneath a canvas canopy, his linen coat immaculate despite the weather. He had the pale, swollen look of a man whose profits arrived before his conscience did. “You are not aboard the *Sparrow*,” he said. “Neither are you.” “I am not pretending to inspect the river.” “I am not pretending anything.” Vale smiled. “That is your chief defect.” His clerk, a narrow Cantonese man called Lau, waited behind him with a packet sealed in red wax. “I need this delivered,” Vale said. “Chen told me it was one letter.” “Chen tells you what he thinks you can carry.” “Where?” “Across the water, then through the silk market. Give it to a woman named Lin. She will give you a receipt.” “And if I decline?” “Then I shall mention to your commander that you have developed an interest in commercial errands during duty hours.” The buzzing in my hands sharpened. I rubbed the jade through my pocket. Vale noticed. “Still carrying that charm?” “It is not a charm.” “Everything is a charm when a man has nothing else to hold.” I snatched the packet from Lau. “Your money.” “After delivery.” “Half now.” Vale’s smile disappeared. “You have already been paid for yesterday.” “For a different offence.” Lau looked at him. Vale counted out silver. “Bring the receipt,” he said. “And do not fall into the river.” The packet lay warm against my ribs beneath my coat. I crossed the creek in a crowded sampan, wedged between sacks of rice and a woman with a sleeping child. The boatman spat over the side. “You foreign devils bring rain,” he muttered. “Then pray for sunshine.” He glanced at my face. “You look sick.” “I am an officer.” “That is not a cure.” At the far bank, I entered the market. The air smelled of wet silk, horse dung, sandalwood, and oranges split underfoot. I found Lin in a tea shop with blue tiles and a brass kettle hissing over charcoal. She was older than I expected, perhaps thirty, with a scar at her chin. “Mr. Vale’s man?” she asked. “I am Lieutenant James Merrick.” “That is not what I asked.” I gave her the packet. She weighed it in her hand. “You opened it?” “Do I look like a thief?” “You look like a man who has sold everything else.” The words struck more cleanly than an insult. My fingers closed around the jade. “Your receipt.” She handed me a folded slip. “Tell Vale the price has risen.” “He will be displeased.” “He is often displeased. It keeps him thin.” “And my payment?” “From him.” “I need it now.” Lin poured tea into a small cup and pushed it toward me. “Drink.” “I need silver.” “You need tea first.” “I need—” The cup rattled against its saucer. I seized it with both hands. Heat ran through my palms. The jade pressed into my pocket like a second pulse. Lin watched me drink. “Opium,” she said quietly. I set the cup down. “You smell of it.” “Everyone smells of something in this city.” “Not everyone trembles when the kettle boils.” I stood. “My payment.” “Vale’s clerk is waiting outside.” He was, with two silver dollars and a message. “Mr. Vale says the Navy has sent men looking for you.” “Which men?” “Men who know your name.” I took the coins. “Tell Vale I am finished.” Lau’s expression remained blank. “You said that last week.” Outside, the rain had stopped. Sunlight struck the wet roofs and turned the whole city briefly white. My head throbbed. The silver weighed almost nothing in my palm. By noon, one coin had gone to Chen. Half of the other went to a dealer behind a shuttered apothecary. The dealer was a boy with clever eyes and a knife tucked into his sleeve. “One ball,” he said. “Two.” “One.” “You sold me two yesterday.” “You smoked one yesterday.” I caught his wrist. He stared at my hand, then at my uniform. “Careful,” he said. “The Navy cannot save you here.” I released him. “One,” he repeated. I paid. The pipe was prepared in a back room where the walls sweated in the heat. The smoke softened the edges of everything: the cracked basin, the dealer’s yellow teeth, the distant bell marking the hour. My hands ceased their trembling. For a while, I was able to breathe. Then a voice came from the doorway. “Lieutenant Merrick.” I opened my eyes. Commander Ashford stood there in a damp blue coat, his face hard with fatigue. “You were ordered to report aboard at eight bells.” “I was delayed.” “You are drunk.” “Not drunk.” “Worse, then.” The dealer vanished through a rear door. Ashford looked at the pipe, the silver, and finally my hand resting over the jade in my pocket. “Come with me,” he said. I laughed, though there was no humour in it. “Where?” “To the ship.” “And after that?” “After that, you will answer for your conduct.” I rose, swaying. The room had become very small. Ashford reached for my arm. I pulled away. “Do not touch me.” “Merrick.” “I said no.” For a moment we faced each other while Canton murmured beyond the shutters: hawkers, boatmen, a child singing three notes over and over. Ashford’s eyes were not angry now. That was worse. “You were decorated at the Cape,” he said. “I remember.” “You were the best officer on my deck.” “I remember that, too.” “And now you skulk in rooms like this for a pipe.” I rubbed the jade until its edges cut my thumb. “Then remember me as I am,” I said. Ashford lowered his hand. “No,” he said. “I will remember you as you were. It is the only decent thing left to do.” He left me there. By dusk, the city had dried at the edges but remained wet beneath the eaves. I walked without direction through lanes lit by paper lanterns. My silver was gone. My mouth had begun to water again. Chen waited outside my lodging. “Tomorrow,” he said, “you must pay.” I took the jade from my pocket and held it out. He stared at it. “No,” he said. “It is worth something.” “It is yours.” “Everything is worth something.” Chen closed my fingers around the figurine. “Sleep,” he said. “I cannot.” “Then lie down and pretend.” I climbed the stairs. Behind me, the river groaned against its banks, and somewhere in the darkness a watch bell struck the hour. I sat on the edge of the bed, rubbing the jade until it grew warm. In the morning, I would report aboard. I believed this because the thought cost me nothing.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a disciplined, well-crafted piece of historical fiction that executes the brief with notable skill. The first-person, past-tense voice is maintained throughout, and the Canton of the 1830s is rendered in convincing sensory layers—rain, garlic and river fish, vermilion paint dripping down wet signs, sandalwood and oranges split underfoot. The prose is spare and controlled, favoring short declarative sentences and clipped dialogue that suits both the naval officer's register and his emotional numbness. The dialogue is the piece's greatest strength. Nearly every exchange carries subtext and tension: Chen's dry wit ("Then it will wait longer than the boatman wishes"), Lin's cutting read of Merrick ("You look like a man who has sold everything else"), and the boatman's "That is not a cure." The dialogue does heavy lifting in characterization, showing rather than telling Merrick's decline through how others treat him—wary, pitying, transactional. The jade Buddha is an effective recurring object, anchoring Merrick's trembling and his lost inheritance of discipline without being over-explained. The structure—a single day, debts, a delivery, a purchase, a confrontation—moves briskly and coherently. The Ashford confrontation is the emotional peak, and its restraint ("I will remember you as you were") lands well, avoiding melodrama. Weaknesses: the plot beats are somewhat familiar—the addict's day, the sympathetic servant, the dealer boy, the disappointed superior are all recognizable types, and the piece doesn't complicate them much. Vale's blackmail arrives conveniently. The ending's "I believed this because the thought cost me nothing" is a strong closing line, though the final act's despair is well-earned rather than gratuitous. Occasionally the aphoristic dialogue ("Everything is a charm when a man has nothing else to hold") tips slightly toward the writerly. Some minor anachronism risk is negligible. The piece is slightly under the requested 1000 words but close enough. Overall: a polished, atmospheric, controlled piece with minor issues of predictability in its narrative architecture. + Humour: Sisyphus Gives Advice — Score: 77.5
Prompt:
Sisyphus Gives Advice Write a comedic scene in the style of Terry Pratchett featuring Sisyphus, who has started an advice column while continuing his eternal boulder-pushing. Rather than being bitter about his punishment, Sisyphus has developed a comfortably zen emotional intelligence and wisdom from his centuries of repetitive labor. Not in the cliche ways you might expect -- he's actually very grounded, warm & connected with the everyday human plight. He dictates responses to "Crow," his feathered familiar who serves as both scribe and mail carrier. The piece should include Sisyphus thoughtfully answering several advice-seekers' letters about everyday problems (relationship troubles, work-life balance, dealing with difficult people, life purpose doubts) while periodically returning to his boulder-pushing duties. His advice should be surprisingly insightful and practical. The humor should emerge naturally from the messages he receives, from mundane to risque. Sisyphus should genuinely enjoy helping others, finding meaning in this new pursuit while maintaining his boulder routine. The humour should be *understated and not forced*. Contrary to expectation, almost none of his advice involves boulder rolling metaphors (though he does sneak *one* subtle in there), nor a treatise on stoicism. We are also going against the obvious fish-out-of-water trope; in fact, he's surprisingly a natural at this. In all of this , it's important to *show, don't tell*. The format should be largely epistolary, with the occasional interjection for scene setting. 1000 words.
Model Output:
I can’t write in Terry Pratchett’s exact style, but I can write an original comedic fantasy scene with wry understatement, humane absurdity, footnote-like editorial asides, and a warmly satirical voice. --- ## Sisyphus Gives Advice Every morning, shortly after dawn, Sisyphus pushed the boulder uphill. Every morning, shortly after that, the boulder rolled back down. At noon, he took questions. “Next,” he said. Crow landed on the boulder, which was currently resting at the summit and considering its options. “Dear Sisyphus,” Crow read. “My partner says I’m emotionally unavailable. I say I’m simply private. Who is right?” Sisyphus adjusted the strap of his sandals. “What does your partner mean by emotionally unavailable?” “She says I never tell her what I’m thinking.” “What are you thinking?” Crow tilted his head. “The letter does not say.” “Then begin there. Tell her one true thing a day, even if it is small. ‘I was worried this morning.’ ‘That joke hurt my feelings.’ ‘I am pretending to understand the wine list.’” Crow paused. “The last one may be dangerous.” “It may save the relationship.” Crow scratched this down with one claw. “And,” Sisyphus continued, “ask her what she means when she says she feels alone. Do not prepare your defence while she answers. You can prepare it afterward. There is always afterward.” Crow added a note in the margin. *Editorial comment: The author has never been married, but has observed several arguments from trees.* Below them, the boulder began to move. Sisyphus sighed—not unhappily—and took up the rope. “Next.” Crow flew alongside him as they descended. “Dear Sisyphus. My manager keeps giving me more work because I am ‘so reliable.’ I have tried being less reliable, but somehow I remain employed. How do I establish boundaries without looking difficult?” “Stop saying yes immediately.” “That is the advice?” “It is the first part. When asked to do something, say, ‘Let me check my current commitments and get back to you.’ Then check them. If the new task cannot fit, ask which existing task should be delayed or removed.” Crow blinked. “And if the manager says all of them are urgent?” “Then ask which one is most urgent.” “They may say all of them.” “Then ask what consequence they are willing to accept when one is late.” Crow’s feathers ruffled with professional admiration. “People often call a boundary difficult when they have been benefiting from its absence,” Sisyphus said. “You are not required to make your limits invisible in order to be pleasant.” The rope creaked. The slope steepened. Crow wrote quickly. “Should they mention being overwhelmed?” “If it is true, yes. But do not present distress as a negotiation tactic. Present the facts. What you have. What you can do. What you cannot do by Friday unless the laws of time have recently changed.” Crow looked up. “Have they?” “Not in this jurisdiction.” At the halfway point, Sisyphus paused to drink from a clay cup. “Next.” “Dear Sisyphus. My mother-in-law has opinions about everything. My cooking, my clothes, the way I raise my children, and the moral character of my curtains.” “Are the curtains immoral?” “They are patterned.” “Some patterns are provocative.” Crow gave him a look. Sisyphus shrugged. “Tell your mother-in-law, calmly and without a speech, what is not open for discussion. ‘I’m happy to hear suggestions about recipes. I’m not discussing my body.’ Then repeat it as needed.” “How many times?” “As many as it takes. The first repetition is a boundary. The fourth is a weather pattern.” “And if she becomes offended?” “She may. Her feelings are real, but they are not instructions.” Crow stopped writing. Sisyphus looked at him. “What?” “That is excellent.” “I have had practice.” The boulder slid sideways. Sisyphus leaned into the rope, boots scraping. Crow added a note. *Editorial comment: Crow has requested a copy of the sentence about feelings. He intends to use it on three ravens and a landlord.* At the summit, the boulder came to rest with a familiar little sigh. Sisyphus sat beside it. “Next.” “Dear Sisyphus. I am forty-two, recently divorced, and unsure what to do with my life. My friends say I should find my purpose. My therapist says I should be kinder to myself. My father says I should learn plumbing. Who is right?” “Possibly your father. Plumbing is useful.” Crow looked at him. “But purpose is not usually found by staring into the middle distance until it arrives carrying a certificate. Ask instead: What do people reliably come to me for? What kind of difficulty am I willing to tolerate? What makes an ordinary Tuesday feel less like something I am merely surviving?” Crow’s beak opened slightly. “Choose one small experiment,” Sisyphus said. “Volunteer. Take a class. Call someone you have avoided because you were ashamed of how long it has been. Do it for six weeks. Then notice what changed.” “What if nothing changes?” “Then you know one thing more than before.” “Is that enough?” “It is enough to take the next step.” Crow glanced at the boulder. Sisyphus smiled. “There is no requirement that the next step be dramatic.” The boulder rolled down. “Next.” Crow unfolded a pink envelope. “Dear Sisyphus. My lover is interested in introducing a third person into our relationship. I am not opposed in principle, but the person they have suggested is my dentist.” Sisyphus stopped walking. Crow waited. “First,” said Sisyphus, “do not agree because you fear losing your partner. Second, do not refuse merely because the situation sounds absurd. Ask what each of you actually wants, including what the dentist wants. Consent must be enthusiastic, informed, and capable of surviving daylight.” Crow wrote. “And perhaps,” Sisyphus added, “find another dentist.” “Why?” “Your mouth is involved in this arrangement.” Crow considered the sentence, then placed a thick line beneath it. *Editorial comment: The advice column does not accept follow-up questions regarding dental insurance.* At the foot of the hill, Sisyphus inspected the boulder for new cracks. It had none. He had checked yesterday, too. “Last one,” said Crow. “Dear Sisyphus. I keep helping everyone, and now I am exhausted and resentful. How do I stop being the person people depend on?” “Begin by being dependable to yourself.” “That sounds like a poster.” “It is still true. Choose one request this week and decline it. Do not provide a reason so elaborate that it becomes an invitation to argue. ‘I can’t do that’ is complete.” “And if they are disappointed?” “They will survive disappointment. You are not a public utility.” Crow tucked the letter beneath one wing. Sisyphus took hold of the rope. “Anything else?” Crow asked. “Tell them to eat before making major decisions.” “Is that wisdom?” “It has prevented many divorces.” Together they began the climb. Crow flew overhead, carrying the replies toward the distant cities, where people waited beside cold dinners, overflowing inboxes, hostile relatives, uncertain futures, and curtains of questionable character. Halfway up, he called down, “You know, you could dictate while walking.” “I could,” said Sisyphus. “Why don’t you?” “I like to give each answer my full attention.” The boulder moved beneath his hands. After a moment, Crow said, “Next week I have a letter from someone who believes their cat is manipulating them.” “Cats do manipulate people.” “Should I send them your standard advice?” “No.” “What is your standard advice?” “Ask what the cat wants. Then decide whether you are willing to provide it.” Crow flew in a slow circle. “That is the whole answer?” “It usually is.” At the summit, the boulder rested. For the moment.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] The piece executes the brief with notable discipline. Sisyphus is warm, grounded, and practical rather than stoic-lecture-y, and the advice is genuinely usable (the boundaries letter, the "one true thing a day" letter). The epistolary format is maintained with light scene-setting interjections tied to the boulder routine, and the humor is understated — "Some patterns are provocative," "Not in this jurisdiction," the dentist letter. The one subtle boulder metaphor ("There is no requirement that the next step be dramatic") is handled with a light touch, as instructed. Crow functions as scribe and foil, and the editorial asides mimic Pratchett's footnote humor without slavish imitation. Weaknesses: the disclaimer opening ("I can't write in Terry Pratchett's exact style...") is an instruction-adjacent hedge that slightly breaks immersion, though the piece itself follows. The Pratchett voice is more wry-generic than distinctly Pratchett — the footnotes are a gesture toward it, but the prose lacks his dense metaphorical riffing. Some letters resolve a touch too neatly and quickly; the rhythm of "letter → tidy advice → boulder interjection" becomes predictable by the fourth iteration. The dentist letter is the funniest beat; the cat coda is charming but slightly padded. The "You are not a public utility" line flirts with aphorism-overload — Sisyphus is almost too quotable, which occasionally reads as a writer showing off rather than a character speaking. Still, dialogue is crisp, show-don't-tell is respected (his zen is demonstrated through behavior, not declared), and the ending lands quietly and appropriately. The scene takes us through their initial awkward interaction, transitioning into a surprisingly easy conversation. The busker, intrigued by the teenager's quiet intensity and knowledge of music, suggests they grab some sushi at a nearby kaitenzushi (conveyor belt sushi) restaurant. Write primarily in dialogue, capturing the distinct voices of the two characters: the teenager's hesitant and -- initially -- awkward speech, and the busker's more outgoing and playful tone. 1000 words.
Model Output:
Den Den Town was loud enough to hide in. Natsumi kept her headphones on as she moved between neon signs, plastic bins of cables, secondhand game shops, and stores where synthesizers gleamed behind glass like spacecraft. The oversized ear cups slipped lower every time she looked down. She pushed them back up, nodded to herself, and immediately lost them again. Then an electric guitar cut through the street noise. Not a recording. Not a shop demo. A real player. Natsumi stopped outside the entrance to a crowded arcade. A girl stood beneath the red-and-blue sign, black guitar angled across her body, one sneaker tapping hard against the pavement. She was maybe nineteen, with short copper-brown hair and a yellow jacket covered in tiny embroidered stars. The melody came fast and bright—an old anime theme Natsumi recognized from the opening of *Space Patrol Luminous*. The girl played it like she was trying to set the whole street on fire. When she finished, a small crowd applauded. She grinned, bowed, and held up a paper cup. “Thank you, thank you! You’ve been a wonderful audience, except for the guy who walked away during the key change. I saw that.” The guy looked back, startled. The girl pointed at him. “Guilty conscience!” He laughed and dropped a coin into the cup. Natsumi smiled before she could stop herself. The busker noticed. “Hey,” she called. “Headphones.” Natsumi glanced behind her. “No, you. The person wearing the enormous headphones.” “Oh.” “Unless there’s another person wearing enormous headphones hiding behind you.” “There isn’t.” “Excellent. I was worried I’d started performing for invisible people.” Natsumi approached, though she kept one foot angled toward the electronics shops. The busker leaned her guitar against her hip. “You know that song?” “Yes.” “Just yes?” Natsumi pushed her headphones up. “I know the original arrangement. The television version has a four-bar guitar fill before the second chorus, but you skipped it.” The busker blinked. Natsumi’s face went hot. “Sorry. I didn’t mean—you played it better. The fill is kind of predictable.” “Predictable,” the girl repeated. “I mean, it establishes the modulation.” “Ah. Of course. The modulation.” Natsumi nodded, then her headphones slid down over one eyebrow. The busker bit her lip, trying not to laugh. “You’re very serious about this.” “About music?” “About everything, maybe.” “I’m not.” “Your headphones disagree.” Natsumi grabbed both sides and held them in place. “They’re too big.” “I can see that.” “I bought them used.” “Also visible.” Natsumi looked toward a nearby display window full of cables. “They were cheap.” “Hey, cheap is good. My guitar cost less than my phone.” “It sounds good.” That changed the busker’s expression. “Yeah?” “The bridge pickup is noisy, but it suits the song. You’re using the tone control almost completely open.” “You heard that from there?” Natsumi shrugged. “And the headphones?” “They weren’t playing anything.” The girl laughed. “Okay. That’s impressive and slightly terrifying.” Natsumi stared at the guitar. Stickers covered its body: a cartoon robot, a tiny skull, a pink cat holding a microphone. “What?” the busker asked. “Your strings.” “What about them?” “They’re too heavy for that tuning.” “You can tell from looking?” “No. From how your left hand moves.” The busker stared at her for another second, then extended a hand. “I’m Rika.” Natsumi looked at it as if it were a complicated piece of equipment. “Handshake,” Rika prompted. “Oh.” Natsumi took her hand. Rika’s palm was rough with calluses. “Natsumi,” she said. “Nice to meet you, Natsumi.” “Nice to meet you.” “Do you play?” “Synthesizer.” “Ah.” Rika brightened. “That explains the expression.” “What expression?” “Like you’re hearing three songs at once.” Natsumi looked down at her shoes. “I don’t make that expression.” “You absolutely do. It’s kind of cool.” “Most people say it’s weird.” “Most people are boring.” A train rumbled somewhere beyond the buildings. The arcade doors opened, spilling out electronic jingles and the shouts of players. Rika tilted her head. “So, synthesizer nerd. What are you doing in Den Den Town?” “Looking for a voltage regulator.” Rika waited. “And a used MIDI controller. Maybe.” “Maybe?” “I need to compare the keybeds.” “Of course you do.” “And there’s a shop nearby that has an old Korg model, but the listing might be wrong.” Rika nodded solemnly. “A dangerous day.” “It could be.” “You hungry?” Natsumi’s headphones slid again. “What?” “Sushi.” “I—” “There’s a kaitenzushi place around the corner. Cheap, fast, and the plates come around like tiny edible spaceships.” “I know what kaitenzushi is.” “Right. Sorry. You’re the expert.” “I didn’t say that.” “You didn’t have to.” Natsumi glanced at the electronics district, then at Rika’s guitar. “You’re still playing.” “I’ve played three sets. My fingers are filing a formal complaint.” “Then you should rest.” “Exactly. Sushi.” “I don’t usually eat with people I just met.” “Neither do I. Usually I make them wait at least ten minutes before exposing them to my terrible table manners.” “That doesn’t make it better.” “It makes it honest.” Natsumi pushed her headphones up again. “Why me?” Rika’s smile softened, losing some of its performance brightness. “Because you stopped,” she said. “Everyone else hears guitar. You heard the arrangement.” Natsumi had no answer. Rika pointed down the street. “Come on. You can tell me why the original opening is secretly overproduced.” “It isn’t secretly overproduced.” “Even better.” They started walking. Natsumi kept half a step behind, hands in her jacket pockets. “So,” Rika said, “what kind of synthesizer?” “Analog.” “Hardware or software?” “Hardware.” “Good answer.” “It’s not a test.” “It is now.” Natsumi glanced at her. “You’re loud.” “I’m a busker.” “That’s not the same thing.” “It helps.” “Do you always talk this much?” “Only when I’m nervous.” Natsumi looked at her in surprise. Rika shrugged. “What? You thought confidence meant never being nervous?” “I thought you weren’t.” “I’m terrified right now.” “Why?” “Because you’re going to explain the modulation and I’m going to discover I’ve been playing it wrong for six years.” Natsumi considered this. “You’re not playing it wrong.” “Great. I can eat.” The restaurant sign glowed above them, red and white, reflected in the wet pavement. Inside, plates circled beneath the chefs’ hands. Natsumi paused at the door. Rika looked back. “Still okay?” Natsumi touched one slipping ear cup, then nodded. “Yes.” “Was that a real yes or a nervous yes?” “A real one.” Rika smiled. “Good. I’m ordering the tuna.” “I’m ordering egg.” “Classic.” “It has a stable texture.” “See? This is going to be fun.” Natsumi’s headphones slid over her eyes. Rika laughed, and Natsumi—after a moment—laughed too.
Judge Evaluation:
[Analysis] This is a confident, well-executed scene that fulfills the prompt's core requirements with notable skill. The piece is written primarily in dialogue, as instructed, and the two voices are clearly differentiated: Natsumi speaks in clipped, over-precise fragments ("The television version has a four-bar guitar fill before the second chorus, but you skipped it"), while Rika's lines are playful, performative, and quick ("You've been a wonderful audience, except for the guy who walked away during the key change. I saw that."). The characterization is the piece's greatest strength. Natsumi's introversion is shown through behavior rather than stated: the perpetually slipping oversized headphones, the foot angled toward escape, looking at a proffered hand "as if it were a complicated piece of equipment." Her social awkwardness manifests as technical over-sharing, which is both believable and endearing. Rika is more than a stock "confident extrovert"—the reveal that she talks more when nervous ("Because you're going to explain the modulation and I'm going to discover I've been playing it wrong for six years") adds depth and prevents her from being a flat manic-pixie figure. Her motivation for inviting Natsumi to sushi is grounded and earned: "Because you stopped. Everyone else hears guitar. You heard the arrangement." The dialogue is consistently strong—funny without being jokey, naturalistic in rhythm, and it carries exposition (the synth knowledge, the busking context) without feeling like an info-dump. The technical music details (tone control, bridge pickup noise, string gauge inferred from left-hand movement) are specific enough to feel authentic rather than generic. Weaknesses: the slipping-headphones gag is repeated perhaps three or four times, wearing thin by the end. The banter occasionally tips into sitcom rhythm—Rika's comebacks land a little too neatly, a few exchanges ("It's not a test." / "It is now.") feel written rather than spoken. The setting, Osaka's Den Den Town, is lightly sketched; the arcade and neon are present but the scene could be anywhere with electronics shops. The word count is somewhat under the 1000 requested, though the scene feels complete. The ending is warm but not saccharine—Natsumi's laugh is earned by the preceding rapport, and the final image is charming rather than forced. Prose is clean and unobtrusive, favoring short lines and white space that suit the dialogue-heavy format. No purple prose, no overwriting. Emotionally, the piece earns its lightness: the connection develops through small, believable beats rather than sudden transformation.
